sections.title: Acknowledgements
sections.html:
Every book accumulates debts that do not appear on its cover.

My first debt is to God, whose grace is the subject of these pages and whose Word supplied both the questions and the answers explored throughout them.

I remain profoundly indebted to my parents, my late father, Dr Chinwoke C. Mbadinuju (Odera) and Mrs Nnebuogo C. Mbadinuju, whose Christian witness continues to shape my own enquiry into Scripture. This book continues, in my own way, the tradition they established. I specially appreciate Apostle "Uncle" Famous E. Uwumangbe for his wise words, encouragement and contributions to this book.

To my family, I owe the gratitude that belongs to those who live closest to the writing process. Books consume hours that might otherwise have belonged elsewhere. Thank you for the patience, encouragement and space that allowed this enquiry to take shape.

I am grateful also to the pastors, teachers, friends and fellow believers whose conversations, questions and disagreements have sharpened my thinking over the years. Some questions entered these pages because somebody was willing to ask them plainly. Others became clearer because somebody refused an easy answer.

My appreciation extends to everyone involved in the work of the Chinwoke Mbadinuju Foundation (CMF) and the continuation of its Remembrance Series. The decision to make digital copies of the books freely available to read on our website cm.foundation follows the principle my late father practised throughout his own writing ministry: the message should travel as widely as Providence permits, without price or location becoming a barrier to the reader.

sections.title: Foreword
sections.html:
For many years, I have preached the Gospel believing that anyone who professes to know God must demonstrate that faith through the life he lives. Christianity demands more than a confession of the lips. It calls for repentance, holiness, obedience and service to God and humanity. I have taught my congregation that genuine faith must bear good fruit, and I stand by that teaching.

Then I encountered the title A Criminal in Heaven.

I must confess that it made me pause.

A criminal in Heaven? What manner of message was the author seeking to convey? How could a man condemned for his wrongdoing receive the promise of Paradise? And what of those who had preached, prophesied and performed wonderful works in Christ's name, only to hear Him declare that He never knew them?

These questions touched my ministry and the responsibilities of preaching. I have urged believers to live godly lives, serve others faithfully and abound in good works. If God Himself requires these things, how could those who presented such works before Christ be denied entrance into Heaven, while a condemned criminal received His promise of Paradise?

This deserved closer examination.

Both accounts are recorded in Scripture, and neither can be disregarded. When the Word of God challenges something we have long believed or taught, we owe it to ourselves and those we lead to search the Scriptures diligently, however unsettling.

Familiarity with Scripture carries a danger: we may overlook the depth of passages we have read and preached for years. We teach established doctrines, explain familiar accounts and encourage others to live by them. Every minister must remain a student of the Word, regardless of how long he has preached.

No preacher has exhausted the wisdom of God.

I appreciate my younger brother Cheta's willingness to examine questions many Christians hesitate to express. His legal training is evident in his careful examination of Scripture and the conclusions drawn from it. He allows Scripture to speak for itself, even when it challenges our understanding.

My teaching concerning good works remains unchanged. Christ expects us to love our neighbours, care for those in need, uphold righteousness and demonstrate our faith through obedience. Heaven cannot be purchased with these works, but I cannot imagine a genuine Christian life in which they have no place.

We must understand why Christ commands righteous living, yet warns that even remarkable religious accomplishments may not secure His approval.

For me, the question remains: if we are commanded to do good works, why were those who appealed to their works rejected? And how did a dying criminal, with no opportunity to establish a record of service, receive the promise of Paradise?

This book deserves reading with these questions in mind.

My prayer is that readers will approach it with humility and an open Bible. Ministers should remember that there is always more to learn from Scripture. Believers should examine their faith, conduct and relationship with Christ. Those seeking God should find encouragement to approach Him sincerely.

I commend this work and pray that it will deepen our understanding of salvation, strengthen our commitment to godly living and draw us into closer fellowship with Jesus Christ, through whom we receive the gift of eternal life.

Apostle Famous E. Uwumangbe
Presiding Pastor,
Jesus Foundation Bible Church International
Benin City, Edo State

sections.title: Preface
sections.html:
A criminal in heaven?

The proposition sounds, at first, like a failure of divine justice. As a lawyer, I instinctively ask what became of his guilt, whether his punishment was deserved and whether anyone suffered because of what he did. As a Christian, I cannot dismiss the difficulty. Jesus Christ Himself promised this condemned man a place in Paradise.

Then I hear another answer from the same Christ. People call Him Lord and point to remarkable works they say they have done in His name. They expect Him to receive them, but He refuses.

Why?

The two encounters have troubled me for different reasons. The criminal admits that his punishment is just, then receives a promise he could never earn. The others believe they have something substantial to present, only to discover that their appeal does not secure the welcome they expect. Both answers came from Christ. I could not set either aside.

Grace is a familiar word to me. I have spoken about it and heard sermons on it. I have leaned on it in prayer. The criminal’s promise made me reconsider what I was really asking others to believe whenever I used that word. His guilt did not disappear when he turned to Jesus. If people had suffered because of his wrongdoing, Christ’s welcome did not undo their loss.

Nor could the man offer a future record in his defence. He had no years left in which to repair what he may have damaged or show how differently he would live. Whatever explains his welcome has to begin with his admitted guilt. The promise came anyway.

The other encounter resists an easy explanation too. The people in Christ’s account call Him Lord. They speak of prophecy and wonderful works done in His name. We know what they claim and what Christ says in reply. We do not know the private history of each person among them. So I would want to understand their expectation of being received before I judge it.

It is easy to move from saying that a deed matters to believing it must settle the question before us. The slide is understandable. In ordinary life, conduct has consequences. We hold people responsible for wrongs and recognise faithful service. Someone helped by a charitable act has good reason to value it. Someone injured by another person has good reason to demand that the injury be taken seriously.

We do not leave those distinctions at the door when we open the Bible. The harder question is what they establish when a person stands before Christ. At what point does “I have tried to live well” become “therefore I have a claim on God?” Can religious service become the ground of a similar confidence? These questions concern entitlement. They concern, too, the good we rightly see in human lives.

I write as a Christian and as a lawyer. Legal practice taught me to listen to a claim before deciding what it proves. It taught me to separate the facts from the inferences drawn from them, and to take an objection seriously even when I expect to disagree with it. Those habits shape this enquiry, though they give me no authority over Christ’s words.

I want to hear the criminal without making him more respectable than the passage allows. I also want to hear the people who address Christ as Lord without assuming, from the outset, that everything they claim to have done was useless. Each case has to be felt at full strength. Otherwise, we risk making Christ’s answers easier to accept by changing the questions to which He gave them.

Readers will come to these passages with different convictions. Some know Calvary’s account so well that the criminal’s welcome no longer surprises them. Others will see their own confidence in the claimants’ appeal, and ask why years of faithful service should not count in their favour.

I ask you to stay with these questions. Pious phrases can close them too quickly, and a strongly felt objection can pass for an answer. Let us read the passages slowly, and notice what they leave unsaid before deciding what follows from Christ’s words.

Crucial questions guide this book’s enquiry: How could the guilty man be welcomed, and why were the claimants refused? Where do obedience and good works belong, if they cannot secure God’s welcome? Why does Scripture still speak of judgment according to works? And what should grace produce in a person who has years to live, not the criminal’s remaining hours?

Each account will be examined in its own setting. They however confront us with questions we recognise. Who deserves mercy? What warrants confidence before God? Before turning to Calvary and Christ’s other verdict, we must consider why these questions trouble us at all.

We may find that our judgments fail in both directions. We may deny hope to someone Jesus Christ would receive, and draw reassurance from the very things He will not accept. If that is so, the criminal is not the only one whose case needs reviewing.

The more unsettling question comes closer to home. Would our confidence in the lives we have lived and the things we have achieved withstand Christ’s judgment?

All biblical quotations in this book are from the King James Version. Its language is part of my own formation; I make no claim that faithful enquiry is confined to one English translation.

sections.title: Prologue
sections.subtitle: The Angst at Apparent Contradictions
sections.html:
We live in an age that understands the language of merit and deserving, justice and consequences. We want our lives to count, our efforts recognised, our sacrifices remembered and wrongdoing taken seriously. Beneath many of our judgments lies a familiar question: what has this person done to deserve this outcome?

Much of ordinary life depends on the answer. A record of faithful service may open doors. A history of dishonesty may close them. We examine what people have done because their conduct gives us reason to trust them or to hold them accountable.

Technology has given those records a reach they once lacked. An old offence can return to public view within minutes, while a forgotten achievement can emerge and change someone’s reputation. Years after an event, a person may still be answering for it.

We understand the value of such scrutiny, but we feel its weight differently when our own record comes under examination. Then we want mitigating circumstances considered, motives understood and one failure weighed against years of effort. The understanding we seek for ourselves can become harder to offer when someone else’s wrongdoing has wounded us.

When our thoughts turn to judgment before God, the stakes change. Surely wrongdoing must matter, and surely faithfulness must matter too. But when we ask who will be with Christ beyond death, how much can a person’s record tell us?

Long before I could frame that question, I watched people whose lives were shaped by that hope. As a restless young boy in the 1980s, I saw my parents become immersed in church life. My father served as our church’s national legal adviser, while the adults around them organised evangelism, attended night vigils and gathered for crusades lasting several days.

I did not always share their enthusiasm for those gatherings. There were places I would rather have been and things I would rather have been doing. Their conviction still intrigued me. People with jobs, families and demanding responsibilities gave their time, strength and resources to a future they could not see.

Heaven meant more to them than a comforting phrase spoken after a death. Being with Christ was worth waiting for and worth living for. Their worship and service gave that expectation a visible place in everyday life.

Years later, as a law student in London, I spent the last night of 1999 with childhood friends beside the River Thames. We watched the crowds, waited for the midnight fireworks and argued about whether the Y2K computer problem would cause systems to fail when the year changed.

I enjoyed the evening, but my thoughts briefly travelled home. The approach of midnight called up an expectation I had heard discussed repeatedly in my younger years, that Christ might return at the turn of the century. I said nothing about it to my friends. Amid the celebrations, though, that earlier world of worship, warnings and hope returned to me for a moment.

Since then, technology has carried the Gospel far beyond the gatherings I remember. Larger churches and conventions bring multitudes together, while broadcasts take worship, preaching and reported miracles to viewers across continents. What once required a journey to a crusade ground can now enter a home through a screen.

The scale has changed, but the hope remains recognisable. People still pray, serve, give and make sacrifices because they believe that being with Christ is worth living for. Having witnessed such devotion, I understand why we expect a life of faithfulness to matter when we think about Heaven.

Then we encounter two statements of Jesus Christ that unsettle any easy confidence in our reckoning. To a condemned criminal beside Him, He says:

“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” Luke 23:43

Elsewhere, He speaks of people who call Him Lord and point to works they say were done in His name. His answer is:

“And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” Matthew 7:23

At first, the verdicts seem difficult to reconcile with what we expect. The reaction comes before we have examined either case. We may be uneasy about a guilty man being welcomed, then uneasy again when people who appear to have served Christ are refused. I will not pretend those feelings away before asking what the verdicts mean.

What becomes of justice if the criminal enters? What becomes of deserving if the workers are refused? We cannot relieve the discomfort by doubting one verdict while accepting the other. The same Christ speaks both. Therein lies the angst arising from these apparent contradictions.

Paradise is no small consolation. Christians have held to that hope through illness, persecution or loss; others have made difficult choices because they believed that being with Christ was worth more than what they might gain by turning away from Him.

That is why the promise at Calvary can provoke more than surprise. It concerns the future people have cherished through years of waiting and hoping. And now a condemned criminal is told he will enter Paradise that day. We may believe Christ’s words and still find ourselves asking:

The same Paradise? So soon?

We should let the questions stand. They show how much the promise means to us, and how difficult it can be to welcome mercy when it lands on someone we would have expected to remain outside.

The other verdict troubles us in a different way. Those who are rejected do not present themselves as strangers to Jesus. They call Him Lord and speak of what they have done in His name. We can understand why they expect to be received; their plea would sound persuasive to many of us.

Perhaps we would be more comfortable if the accounts were less demanding. We could imagine that the criminal was wrongly convicted, or that the people who spoke of wonderful works had never done anything useful. Neither assumption is supplied by the passages. We should take the evidence as Scripture gives it.

Here the language of deserving begins to fail us. We understand why wrongdoing should have consequences and why service should be recognised. How, then, does Christ promise Paradise to a man whose guilt is real, while refusing people who expect their works to count in their favour? What does He see that our judgments have missed?

We welcome the thought that God forgives until the person He receives is someone we know to be guilty. Then the questions become harder. Does mercy leave the wrong unanswered? What of those who suffered because of it? How can the Judge who sees everything promise Paradise to such a man and remain just? Therein lies the scandal of grace.

The scandal of entitlement emerges when Christ refuses those we might expect Him to receive. They call Him Lord and cite works they say were done in His name. Anyone who has tried to live well may recognise their confidence. Why does believing that goodness matters become unsafe when we make it the basis of God’s welcome?

What, then, does Christ mean when He says, “I never knew you”? What does He mean by doing the Father’s will? We must hear those words alongside the plea of people who expected their works to speak for them.

We begin with the criminal himself. What do we know about him, and how much have we assumed? Why does he turn to Jesus when death is so near? What do his words disclose about the way he sees himself and the Man dying beside him? His response matters, but it cannot carry the whole enquiry. The promise also rests on who Jesus is and what His death accomplishes, so we must look to the Man on the middle Cross.

Even then, another question remains. Why does mercy shown to this man make us uncomfortable? Scripture records other occasions when God’s actions surprised people who thought they understood what should happen. Our discomfort may tell us something about God’s ways, or only about the expectations we bring to them.

From there the enquiry turns to the people we might have expected Christ to receive. Their claims of religious service have to be tested, and so does the moral difference between a person who has tried to live well and one whose wrongdoing is plain. What can goodness and service establish? At what point do we begin to rely on them for a verdict they cannot secure?

Then the two accounts must be read together. Weighing the criminal’s guilt against the claimants’ works will not tell us what Christ ought to have said. Neither can we set aside our concern for justice and deserving merely because His answers unsettle it. Any answer has to account for both verdicts. It has to explain, too, where obedience belongs and why Scripture speaks of judgment according to works if good works cannot purchase God’s welcome into Paradise.

The criminal had little earthly life left in which to show what following Christ might have meant. Most of us have had more time. So we must ask what grace should produce across those years, without making our achievements the ground of our confidence.

Only then can we take up the question at the centre of this book. Upon what basis does anyone enter the Kingdom of God?

We cannot answer by treating the criminal’s wrongdoing as harmless or the works the claimants report as worthless. The people affected by wrongdoing matter. So do the people helped by faithful work.

Today a person’s record can be found with a few keystrokes or a voice prompt. It helps us make necessary judgments, but it cannot tell us everything about the person before us.

Christ’s verdicts ask us to examine our own lives with equal care. We may struggle with the criminal’s promise while assuming our record would present fewer difficulties. We may be troubled by the fate of the religious claimants while trusting that the good we have done will weigh in our favour. Sooner or later, each of us has to ask what we expect to speak for us when Christ gives His verdict.

But we are not there yet. First we must meet the man at Calvary, where death is near and there is little time left to say anything at all. Before deciding how he could be promised Paradise, we must listen to what he says.

sections.title: Part I
sections.subtitle: The Criminal and the Claimants
sections.html:
Jesus promises a condemned criminal that he will be with Him in Paradise. Elsewhere, He speaks of people who call Him Lord and expect to enter His kingdom. He refuses them.

We know these answers before we have examined either encounter. That knowledge can make us hurry past what the people involved actually say. We may picture the criminal as we remember him from sermons, or assume that the claimants’ confidence must have been plainly foolish because Christ rejected them. In each case, the verdict can begin to replace the account we ought to read.

We must first return to Calvary. Who is the man on the third cross? What do the Gospels tell us about him, and what do they leave unsaid? As death draws near, what does he say to the man beside him, and what does he ask of Jesus? Only after hearing his words can we begin to consider the promise he receives.

We must give the other account the same care. The people in Christ’s warning call Him Lord and point to works done in His name. Why do they expect Him to recognise their appeal? What has Jesus said immediately before describing them, and what exactly does He say when He refuses them? Knowing the outcome gives us no licence to make their case weaker than the one He chose to set before His hearers.

The two encounters take place in different settings. One unfolds during an execution; the other appears in Christ’s teaching about entry into the kingdom of heaven. We should not pretend that the speakers stand together in a single courtroom. Christ’s answers do, however, invite us to consider the two accounts alongside each other, because both concern people who look to Him for welcome.

Their apparent records pull our expectations in opposite directions. One man is under condemnation. The others point to activities that, if heard without Christ’s answer, many people might regard as strong grounds for confidence. Ordinary life has taught us to take wrongdoing seriously and to recognise service. We have good reason to do both.

The people affected by conduct also matter. If someone has done harm, its consequences do not disappear because the person later seeks mercy. If someone has helped others, those beneficiaries do not lose the help they received because a further question is asked about the person who served them. We need not deny either truth to listen to Christ.

Nor should we fill the silences in the passages with convenient assumptions. The Gospels do not provide a full account of the criminal’s earlier life. Christ’s warning does not supply the private history of every person who will call Him Lord. We will consider what the passages disclose and resist making either side easier to accept by inventing what they do not.

Once we have heard both accounts, we can give each difficulty its proper attention. The criminal’s welcome raises a case against grace: what becomes of justice when a person under condemnation is promised Paradise? What of the wrongdoing for which he was condemned, and of those who may have suffered because of it? Chapter 3 will allow those questions their full force.

Chapter 4 will speak in defence of the deserving. Achievement and service can be valuable to those they help, and Scripture commends obedience and good works. Should these things not also matter to God? Whether their value gives a person a claim upon Him is a further question. First, the defence deserves to be heard on its own terms.

Christ speaks of doing His Father’s will, and Scripture speaks of judgment according to works. Those words must eventually be understood alongside His promise to the criminal and His refusal of the claimants. We should hear both accounts and the questions they raise before attempting that answer.

We begin at the third cross. Jesus has promised Paradise to a condemned man. Now, we must hear the man to whom Christ gave it.

sections.title: The Third Cross
sections.html:
Three men were crucified at Calvary. We tend to look towards the middle Cross, as we should. On one of the other crosses, however, hangs a man whose words and promised future raise difficult questions far beyond that afternoon.

The Bible does not give us his name. It tells us nothing of his childhood, his family or the offence that brought him under Roman judgment. We meet him near the end of his life, with little time left in which to explain it.

A fuller history might make him easier to picture. It might also tempt us to find something in his past that would make Christ’s promise easier to explain. Luke leaves most of that history unknown, but he lets us hear what the man says about himself.

What did the man say about his own deeds, and what did he see in Jesus while both were dying? Before we decide what to make of Christ’s answer, we should let him speak.

The Man Beside Jesus

All four Gospels place two other men beside Jesus at His crucifixion. Matthew writes:

“Then were there two thieves crucified with him, one on the right hand, and another on the left.” Matthew 27:38

Mark records the same arrangement. Luke calls the men “malefactors,” while John tells us that Jesus was crucified between them. The position of the three men is clear, though none of these accounts tells us precisely what the man who later appealed to Jesus had done.

Crucifixion was a public death. Soldiers carried out the execution while rulers, passers-by and others watched. The condemned men could hear what was said around them and, while they still had strength, could speak.

Jesus was placed among men being put to death as criminals. Isaiah had written of one who would be “numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12). The arrangement at Calvary made those words visible, whatever else the prophecy may hold.

From a distance, the crosses gave an observer little help. Three men suffered under the same means of execution. The sight alone could not tell anyone whether all three deserved the sentence. Luke allows one of the condemned men to make the distinction. Rebuking his companion, he says:

“And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss.” Luke 23:41

As a lawyer, I know the difference between an accusation and an admission. An accusation may be mistaken. Evidence may be incomplete. A court can reach a wrong conclusion. The criminal’s words do not answer every question about Roman justice, but they tell us how he regards his own case.

“We indeed justly.” He includes himself in the judgment. He accepts that their punishment is deserved, that their own deeds have brought them under condemnation, while insisting that Jesus does not belong in the same category.

We should not turn his admission into a detailed confession Luke never records. We do not know his offence. The Bible does not give us any account of his past. We do know that he makes no claim of innocence when he speaks to the man beside him.

Voices Around the Crosses

The criminal did not begin as a defender of Jesus. Matthew says that the thieves crucified with Him joined in the abuse directed at Him. Mark likewise records:

“And they that were crucified with him reviled him.” Mark 15:32

The people below the crosses spoke in different voices, but their taunts returned to a similar challenge. If Jesus was who He claimed to be, why did He remain there? The rulers mocked Him for saving others while apparently unable to save Himself.

Luke records their words:

“He saved others; let him save himself, if he be Christ, the chosen of God.” Luke 23:35

The soldiers took up the challenge in terms of kingship:

“If thou be the king of the Jews, save thyself.” Luke 23:37

Above Jesus was an inscription naming Him King of the Jews. Those watching could read it while Roman soldiers controlled the place of His execution. The inscription made the question of His kingship public at the very moment His circumstances invited ridicule.

The criminals could hear these voices from their crosses. Matthew and Mark describe the men crucified with Jesus joining the mockery. Luke brings us close enough to hear one continue:

“If thou be Christ, save thyself and us.” Luke 23:39

His words resemble the challenge from below, with an addition that matters to a dying man. He wants Jesus to save them as well. His desperate wish needs no explanation. Luke asks us to notice that the other criminal spoke differently.

Matthew and Mark describe the mockery around the crosses. Luke also records the exchange in which one criminal rebukes the other. The Gospels do not give us a sequence detailed enough to say when the second man’s outlook changed or what brought it about. We need not supply an event that none of them records.

Luke makes the difference audible. The man turns to his companion, who is still railing against Jesus, and asks:

“Dost not thou fear God, seeing thou art in the same condemnation?” Luke 23:40

J. C. Ryle drew attention to the dying man’s rebuke of his companion. Both remain under sentence. Neither has been taken down. One, however, will no longer join the other in speaking against Jesus.

His question introduces God into a scene dominated by Roman power and public contempt. He asks his companion to consider more than the pain of their execution or the opinions of the people below them.

Then he speaks about their own conduct and Jesus’ innocence. He does so with no visible prospect that his words will alter his sentence.

When Self-Defence Ends

People do not always abandon their defence when a sentence becomes inevitable. Some continue to deny what they did. Others admit only what can no longer be disputed, while explaining why another person bears the greater blame.

The criminal had someone beside him with whom he could compare himself. He might have rebuked his companion while suggesting that his own case was different. Instead, he includes himself when he says:

“And we indeed justly.” Luke 23:41

That small word “we” matters. His rebuke concerns their failure to fear God, and his account of their punishment includes his own deeds. He distinguishes Jesus from the condemned men, but makes no claim that his companion is guilty while he is innocent.

An admission can establish responsibility. It cannot, simply by being made, repair the wrong. We should credit his admission for what it is and claim nothing more for it.

He does not say that his admission has earned him a favourable answer. Having spoken truthfully about his deeds, he turns to someone else for help.

More Than Fear of Dying

How much can we infer from words spoken near death? Fear may make a person regret the consequences of wrongdoing without changing his judgment about the wrong itself.

Luke does not reveal the criminal’s private thoughts. We cannot identify when he changed, measure the depth of his feelings or insist that he experienced every aspect of repentance in a form we can reconstruct.

His words nevertheless say more than I wish this had not happened to me. He speaks of fearing God. He accepts that their punishment is deserved and declares that Jesus has done nothing amiss. Those are judgments about conduct, not merely expressions of pain.

David’s confession gives us a familiar comparison:

“For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.” Psalm 51:3

In Jesus’ parable, the returning son says:

“Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son.” Luke 15:21

Neither passage supplies a speech the criminal was required to repeat. They help us recognise the significance of acknowledging a wrong without trying to negotiate an excuse.

There is still a difference between recognising guilt and knowing where to turn with it. The criminal does not finish by describing his deeds. Having spoken about himself and Jesus, he addresses Jesus directly.

A Kingdom at Calvary

The criminal’s request is brief:

“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” Luke 23:42

The words are remarkable in their setting. Jesus remains on the Cross. The inscription above Him names Him a king, while the soldiers and rulers treat that claim as a reason for mockery. Nothing visible has changed to vindicate it.

The other criminal asks Jesus to save them from the crosses. The man who turns towards Him speaks of a kingdom beyond what the three men can presently see. He asks to be remembered there.

We can hear the difference without claiming to know everything behind either request. Both men face death. One asks Jesus to change their immediate circumstances. The other entrusts to Him a future those circumstances appear to have closed.

“Remember me” is a small request to make from a cross. The criminal gives Jesus no account of earlier service and promises Him no years of better conduct. He asks to be kept in mind when Jesus comes into His kingdom.

The request is greater than it sounds. Anyone beside him might offer sympathy for his remaining hours. This man asks Jesus for something beyond death, addressing Him as King while soldiers still control the place of His execution.

John Calvin noted the distance between what the criminal could see and what he asked. He spoke of Christ’s kingdom while Christ appeared overcome by shame and death. That observation returns us to the scene without suggesting that the criminal possessed a complete understanding of later Christian teaching.

We do not know how much he understood about Jesus’ death or what would follow. His words reveal where he placed his hope. Having admitted that his deeds deserved punishment, he entrusted his future to the Man whom the crowd expected to die beside him.

We may call his reliance upon Jesus faith. Luke lets us hear it. Why Christ received him is the question that remains.

Paradise Before Sunset

Luke records no further enquiry into the criminal’s offence. No fresh evidence is brought to Calvary and no later record of obedience is offered. Jesus answers him there:

“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” Luke 23:43

The man asked to be remembered when Jesus came into His kingdom. Jesus promises that he will be with Him, in Paradise, that day.

Notice the certainty of that answer. The criminal is still dying. Jesus does not promise that he may eventually be considered if he can establish a better record. He speaks of a future the man has no means to arrange for himself.

The same man who said “we indeed justly” now hears that he will be with Jesus in Paradise. His admission has not been withdrawn, and no future conduct has been offered. We may rejoice at Christ’s answer and still ask how both statements can stand.

Jesus’ words do not take him down from his cross. John records that the soldiers later broke the legs of the men crucified beside Him. His earthly sentence continued.

Nor does the promise identify his offence or undo its effects. The guilty man remains guilty of the deeds he acknowledged when Christ speaks of Paradise. Luke gives us no reason to soften either side of the account.

The Promise and the Man

The criminal’s remaining hours were not empty. He acknowledged his guilt, challenged his companion, declared Jesus innocent and asked to be remembered. Those words show a turn towards Christ, though Luke does not tell us how he would have lived had more time been given to him.

That response was not the price of Paradise. He did not present his admission or his faith as an achievement that placed Jesus in his debt. He asked for a future he could not secure, and Jesus answered with more than he requested.

A guilty man remained on his cross while Christ promised that he would be with Him in Paradise. We have heard what this man brought to Jesus. Elsewhere, people bring Him an impressive account of works done in His name. What does He say to them?

sections.title: Lord, Lord
sections.html:
“Lord, Lord.”

Jesus says that many will address Him this way when entry into the kingdom of heaven is at issue. They will point to remarkable works done, they say, in His name and expect Him to recognise their claim.

The man at Calvary asked only to be remembered. These people come with an account of what they have done. If we heard their appeal before knowing Christ’s answer, would we expect Him to turn them away?

We should listen to the passage in the setting in which Jesus gave it. What does He say about doing His Father’s will? Why do the claimants repeat “in thy name,” and what do they believe those words establish? When Christ answers them, we must hear everything He says, even before we are ready to explain it.

The criminal’s offence was not named, but he admitted his guilt. The claimants name their works with confidence. Their case gets the same hearing we gave his.

The Sermon’s Closing Warning

Jesus speaks these words near the close of the Sermon on the Mount. He has taught about anger, reconciliation, truthfulness, prayer, possessions and the way people treat one another. His hearers have been given much to consider about a life lived before God and among other people.

As the Sermon draws towards its end, Jesus speaks of a narrow way and warns against false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing. He tells His hearers that they will know such people by their fruits. His warning about those who call Him Lord follows in that setting.

This makes the claimants’ appeal more arresting. They do not present an empty account. They name activities that many observers would consider persuasive evidence of a connection with Jesus.

He has already told His hearers to look closely. What people do matters. An impressive appearance may need a second look. We should bring that scrutiny to the claimants, though we cannot know their private histories.

Jesus says:

“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” Matthew 7:21

The first words prevent us from treating a profession of faith as conclusive. Calling Jesus “Lord,” even with emphasis, cannot by itself settle the question of entry.

The rest of the sentence matters just as much. Jesus speaks of doing His Father’s will. The criminal’s welcome gives us no permission to pass over that clause, and we have not yet explained everything it means.

Consider again how the sentence is built. Jesus does not say merely that those who refuse to acknowledge Him will be turned away. He warns that some who address Him as Lord will not enter.

That is already an uncomfortable prospect. Many of us know how to recognise open rejection. We may be less prepared for a person who speaks reverently to Christ, expects His welcome and is nevertheless mistaken.

Jesus then tells us what many will say to Him:

“Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?” Matthew 7:22

Their appeal goes well beyond the address “Lord, Lord.” They name three kinds of activity, each connected expressly to Jesus’ name. If their words are the case they bring before Him, we should hear its particulars.

To prophesy in His name is to claim to speak under His authority. To cast out devils in His name is to claim an extraordinary act of deliverance. “Many wonderful works” broadens the account beyond one kind of activity or a single occasion.

Jesus gives us no details by which to investigate any particular claim. We cannot certify the prophecies or the works on the claimants’ behalf, and we cannot dismiss the account as an obvious invention merely because we know Christ’s answer.

They expect Him to draw a conclusion. They believe these activities, joined to their confession of His name, will speak decisively in their favour.

“Have we not?” is a question asked with confidence. They seem to expect Jesus to acknowledge what they have done and agree that it counts for their welcome.

The Case They Bring

Prophecy, casting out devils and many wonderful works are striking things to place before Christ. We can understand why the people who claimed to have done them would expect Him to receive them.

Suppose a client brings a substantial file into my office and says, “Everything you need is here.” The documents may be authentic and show considerable work. I must still ask what they establish about the particular question to be decided.

The claimants also expect their account to settle a question. Their confidence does not make that conclusion sound. It should still keep us from brushing aside the activities they name. Jesus lets us hear their appeal before He gives His answer.

There is a human reason for their confidence. People who have invested themselves in work they regard as important may find an unfavourable judgment difficult to imagine. Here, the work they name is extraordinary, and they say it was done in the name of the very Person they now address.

That expectation may be familiar even to someone who has never prophesied or claimed to cast out a devil. A person may recall responsibilities faithfully carried, sacrifices made or years given to a cause. Those memories need not be false for the person to ask more of them than they can establish.

The comparison has limits. The claimants speak of prophecy, casting out devils and many wonderful works. Jesus tells us no more about the course of their lives. Their appeal has force on the terms they give it, since they believe these acts, done in His name, warrant His welcome.

Jesus says “many” will speak this way. That word should prevent us from treating His warning as a rare curiosity safely confined to people unlike ourselves. Their appeal may fail, but the warning is not theirs alone.

The Verse We Must Not Skip

Before hearing Christ’s response, we must return to His opening sentence:

“…but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” Matthew 7:21

Those words are difficult to hear beside the promise to the criminal. He had no years left in which to establish a record of obedience. Jesus nevertheless speaks here of doing the Father’s will when He describes entry into the kingdom.

The claimants make the difficulty sharper because they are not presenting themselves as inactive. They point to things done in Jesus’ name. The distinction cannot simply be between people who act and people who do nothing.

Nor should we quietly replace “the will of my Father” with whichever activity most impresses us. Jesus’ account requires us to listen before deciding how His words in verse 21 relate to the works named in verse 22.

Matthew Henry noticed the order of the passage. The One who speaks of the Father’s will in verse 21 also hears their plea and gives the answer in verse 23. The claimants cannot decide for Him what their works establish.

Within the Sermon, Jesus has warned against practising righteousness to be seen by others. He has also spoken about fruit, inviting His hearers to consider what a life produces. His concern is with more than a person’s account of impressive acts.

That context tells us nothing of the private history of anyone who says “Lord, Lord.” It does place Jesus’ reference to the Father’s will at the centre of the enquiry, and we must keep it there when we hear both the claimants’ words and His.

It would be convenient to decide here that the criminal’s case makes obedience irrelevant, or that the claimants’ activities must have been worthless. Neither conclusion follows from what we have read. Jesus’ sentence about the Father’s will and His report of their appeal stand side by side, waiting to be examined.

“In Thy Name”

The claimants repeat the phrase three times. They say they prophesied in Jesus’ name, cast out devils in His name and did many wonderful works in His name. They expect that connection to matter when He hears them.

We can understand why. Their appeal is stronger than a claim to have done impressive things generally. They present the works as acts associated with the very Person deciding whether they may enter His kingdom.

His name is no passing reference in their speech. They return to it with each claim, as though its repetition makes the connection impossible to miss. Whatever questions we may later ask about the works, we should first understand why the speakers thought this was the strongest way to present them.

Jesus has already warned that calling Him “Lord” does not, by itself, settle the question. The claimants now offer further grounds for confidence. We must hear what He says about those grounds.

At Calvary, the criminal offered no comparable list. He asked, “Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom” (Luke 23:42). The difference between his request and the claimants’ appeal is plain. Its meaning remains to be settled.

The Answer They Do Not Expect

Jesus completes the scene:

“And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” Matthew 7:23

The appeal unfolds at the moment of judgment, when the question of entry can no longer be postponed. What they had assumed about their works is now placed before the One whose answer settles the matter.

That is part of the unease of this passage. Their confidence has lasted long enough to be voiced directly to Christ. The refusal comes from the Person they address as Lord, and no onlooker’s misunderstanding explains it.

He does not ask them for more examples, and He does not suggest that a longer list would have succeeded. His answer challenges the confidence with which they brought it.

“I never knew you” cannot mean that He lacked information about them. He has heard what they say and gives His own account of their conduct. What it means for Him to know someone will require closer examination later.

We must also hear the last words, “ye that work iniquity.” The claimants speak of wonderful works. Jesus speaks of iniquity. He tells us nothing of each person’s history. We are still not free to ignore His description of them.

The gap between their words and His warns us against conclusions drawn solely from a person’s account of himself. We hear a confident appeal and a list of activity associated with Christ’s name. We cannot claim to know all that Christ knows about the people speaking.

Jesus follows this passage with the image of two houses. One stands because it is built upon a rock; the other falls because it is built upon sand. He speaks of the difference between hearing His words and doing them.

The image does not settle every question raised by the criminal at Calvary. It does prevent us from hearing “Lord, Lord” as though Jesus had no concern for a life shaped by His teaching.

The People We Might Have Admitted

Had we heard only the claimants’ appeal, many of us might have expected Christ to receive them. They call Him Lord and name remarkable works done in His name. His answer is therefore more troubling than a refusal of people who openly rejected Him.

At Calvary, He promised Paradise to a man who admitted that his punishment was deserved. Here, He tells confident claimants, “I never knew you” (Matthew 7:23). We cannot settle the difference by inventing a better past for the criminal or a hidden history for each claimant.

The criminal’s guilt remains after the promise. The claimants speak of works done in Christ’s name. Jesus speaks of doing His Father’s will and calls them workers of iniquity. We must keep both His answers, and all His words in each account, before us.

Many of us would have expected these speakers to enter. Christ’s refusal leaves their expectation unanswered, just as His promise left the criminal’s admitted guilt standing. Before either answer can be explained, we must hear the case against grace. Then we must ask what can be said in defence of the deserving.

sections.title: The Case Against Grace
sections.html:
Two answers from the same Christ now stand before us. He promises Paradise to a man who admits that his punishment is deserved. He refuses people who call Him Lord and point to remarkable works done in His name.

We may be glad for the criminal and uneasy for the claimants. Neither response, however, explains what Christ has said. Before considering whether the claimants deserved a different answer, we must face the difficulty raised by the man who received His promise.

If grace receives the guilty, what becomes of justice? What becomes of the wrong itself, and of those who may have suffered because of it? A quick appeal to mercy will not answer them. Scripture gives them force, and the criminal’s own words make them impossible to avoid.

The Claim of Justice

Scripture does not speak of wrongdoing as a minor flaw God may overlook when compassion moves Him. God’s warning to Adam connects disobedience with death. Ezekiel insists that a person is accountable for his own conduct (Ezekiel 18:20), and Paul writes, “For the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23).

These passages arise in different settings. They should not be arranged as though each were a provision in a single criminal statute. Each refuses to make sin inconsequential.

The criminal speaks of what is due. He says that he and his companion receive “the due reward of our deeds” (Luke 23:41). Whatever remains unknown about his offence, he does not ask Jesus to regard his punishment as a mistake.

That admission carries weight. It comes from the man who is about to receive mercy, not from a spectator determined to deny it to him. He recognises a difference between his own position and that of Jesus, whom he declares to have done nothing amiss.

The difficulty sharpens when God reveals His character to Moses, declaring mercy and forgiveness while affirming that He “will by no means clear the guilty” (Exodus 34:6–7).

Those words do not settle the criminal’s case for us. They rule out any careless explanation of it. If the God who forgives also refuses to treat guilt as nothing, how can the guilty man hear a promise of Paradise?

One answer is that everyone has sinned, and the criminal differs from us only in how visible his wrongdoing was. Paul declares, “For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). We will revisit this when examining our own confidence.

But it cannot be used here to make this man’s conduct disappear into a general account of human imperfection. We do not know what brought him to his cross. We do know that he accepts the punishment as deserved. The question is whether Christ’s welcome can be just while that admission remains true.

The Record We Do Not Have

One way to ease the difficulty would be to find something favourable in the criminal’s earlier life. Perhaps he helped others before the deeds that brought him to Calvary. Perhaps he carried responsibilities faithfully for many years.

We cannot exclude a history Luke has not recorded for us. Nor can we base our explanation upon it. The criminal invokes no virtue from his past, and Jesus requests no account of it before answering his appeal.

Someone may have given generously for years and still owe money taken from another person. Such generosity is worth recognising. The debt remains, and the person owed the money still has an interest in what happens next.

The criminal may have done good. We do not know, and we may not invent further offences either. His admission prevents us from treating Christ’s promise as a reward for an unseen record.

A future record cannot explain it either. He will not leave Calvary to repay debts, repair relationships or demonstrate lasting obedience. Those things count when time remains. They cannot explain a promise to someone dying that day.

Perhaps his final response supplies what is missing. He admits guilt, speaks for Jesus and turns to Him. Those words count, as we have seen. Yet if we make the quality of his admission or the strength of his faith an achievement that earns Paradise, we have found another proposed price without explaining why Christ owes it to him.

His earlier life is largely unknown. His later life will not take place. The words he speaks at Calvary matter, but he does not present them as a defence that Jesus must accept.

We may be tempted to add details because an unexplained welcome unsettles us. A hidden act of kindness would make the man easier to receive. A particularly terrible offence would make him harder. Luke gives us neither. He allows the man’s admission and Christ’s promise to stand beside each other.

Those Who Bear the Harm

One person can disappear when we speak warmly about a wrongdoer receiving mercy. That person is the one harmed by the wrong.

Luke does not identify the criminal’s offence or tell us who suffered because of it. We must not invent a particular victim. The absence of those details does not remove the moral concern.

Suppose a thief is forgiven. The person deprived of property may still need it returned. Suppose a person has betrayed someone who trusted him. His admission may be sincere while the other person continues to live with the loss.

Grace cannot mean that the harmed person is required to say no harm occurred. An account that finds room for the offender but no room for those affected by his deeds has not taken his wrongdoing seriously enough.

In legal practice, a favourable outcome for an accused person does not, by itself, answer a complainant’s account of what happened. The complainant may still ask whether the harm has been acknowledged and what becomes of the loss. Those questions need an answer in their own terms.

The difficulty becomes more searching when the offender can no longer make amends. A person may admit a wrong too late to return what was taken or repair a life altered by it. The admission counts for something. The injured person must still live with what occurred.

The criminal’s execution continues after Jesus speaks. His welcome into Paradise is not a release from his cross or a declaration by Rome that his conviction was mistaken. That distinction answers one question, but leaves another standing.

His punishment does not tell us how his guilt stands before God. Nor does it tell us what Christ’s promise means for someone who may have borne the effects of his deeds. We should not claim more detail than Luke supplies. Nor should we let the missing details make those who suffer harm irrelevant.

Imagine hearing the promise from that person’s position. The condemned man will be with Christ in Paradise that day. You may still be carrying what he did. Would the assurance that he has been forgiven, by itself, answer your concern?

I ask this without suggesting that anyone must be denied mercy because another person has suffered. Any account of mercy worthy of the name must be able to face that suffering. Otherwise, grace begins to sound generous chiefly to the person who did the wrong.

When the Judge Simply Forgives

A human judge who disregarded proven wrongdoing solely because an offender expressed regret at sentencing would face serious questions. Remorse may carry weight. It does not make the offence vanish or settle every claim arising from it.

Scripture itself speaks sharply about wrongful judgment:

“He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.” Proverbs 17:15

The proverb addresses corruption in human judgment. We cannot place it over Christ’s promise as though we had already shown His answer to be corrupt. It does explain why we should hesitate before saying that God simply decided to call a guilty man innocent for no further reason.

Moses says of God: “He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he.” Deuteronomy 32:4

If Christ’s promise expresses God’s judgment, it must accord with God’s character. We cannot resolve the difficulty by suggesting that justice was set aside for an afternoon.

The comparison with a human judge has limits. God is not a magistrate applying a law made by someone else, and Christ is not hearing a conventional appeal against a Roman sentence. Still, the comparison exposes a concern that cannot be waved away. Mercy that can be trusted must face the wrong.

Consider a judge telling a victim, “The offender has sought mercy, so your suffering no longer matters.” Even those inclined towards leniency would recognise the injustice. Mercy towards the offender cannot justify disregard for the person harmed.

That is why the question at Calvary is more difficult than whether Christ has the authority to forgive. It asks how He can exercise that authority without denying what the criminal himself has acknowledged. What gives the harmed person reason to trust the justice of a God who welcomes the wrongdoer?

Paul later speaks of God as “just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). The two descriptions belong together in his sentence. For now, their conjunction sharpens our question. How can God be both when the person He receives is guilty?

At Calvary, Jesus does not deny the criminal’s admission. The man says that his deeds deserve punishment. Jesus promises him Paradise. Both statements stand. We still need to understand how.

A Convenient Last Hour?

There is another objection, one that arises precisely because the promise comes so late. If this man receives Paradise when his life is almost over, might someone conclude that repentance can safely wait until then?

A person could hear the story and reason that there is time to pursue other things now. When death approaches, he might make his own appeal to Christ. If the criminal was received without years of obedience or repair, why should anyone hurry to turn away from wrongdoing?

That is a dangerous conclusion. It is also one we should confront rather than pretend no reader could draw it. A promise meant to display mercy could be misused as an excuse to delay taking guilt seriously.

The criminal had no remaining years in which to choose between following Christ and returning to his former life. Most people who consider postponing repentance do have that choice. The question, then, is whether an exceptional final hour can reasonably be made into a plan for the years before it.

We do not know when our final hour will come, or whether we will be able to speak as clearly as this man did. Beyond that, someone who proposes to seek mercy later because wrongdoing is attractive now has still to face that wrongdoing as the criminal faced his own.

These observations expose the danger without explaining the promise. Can a last-hour welcome make grace sound cheap to those who hear of it earlier in life? Any answer must reckon with anyone tempted to use the criminal’s story as permission to wait.

The Objection Stands

It would be easy to end this chapter by declaring that the Cross answers everything. Christ’s promise requires us to examine the Man on the middle Cross, but pointing towards an answer does not mean we have fully heard the objection.

The criminal’s wrongdoing matters, and so does any person harmed by it. God’s justice matters. So does the danger that someone may misuse this account to put off facing the truth about his own life.

We cannot make the criminal innocent to protect justice, and we cannot make his final words a payment that purchases Paradise. Nor can we assume that his execution settled every question about his guilt before God, or that forgiveness erased whatever consequences others may have borne.

Christ knew whom He was addressing. The man admitted that his punishment was deserved, and Jesus promised him Paradise anyway. If that promise is just, its justice must withstand the questions his admission raises.

Those questions make the case against an easy account of grace. They give us no licence to reject Christ’s words, and none to make His promise smaller than it is.

There is another case still to hear. If wrongdoing must matter, should good conduct and faithful service not matter too? Years of obedience may have cost a person dearly, and the people helped by that service have received something valuable. The people Christ refused expected Him to recognise works done in His name.

We must now ask what can be said in defence of the deserving.

sections.title: In Defence of the Deserving
sections.html:
The criminal has received a promise of Paradise, and the questions raised by his guilt remain before us. But what of the people who have tried to do good? What of those who have served Christ for years and might have expected Him to receive them?

It is easy to hear their questions as complaints against mercy. They need not begin there. We ordinarily believe that conduct matters. Harm calls for an answer, and faithful service earns recognition. The first of those convictions has already had its place in this book; the second is owed the same.

One person appeals to a life of honesty, kindness and upright conduct, without claiming any particular religious achievement. Another points to years of prayer, obedience and service undertaken in Christ’s name. Although the grounds of their confidence differ, both raise a question that deserves careful consideration: should a life devoted to doing good not count for something when Christ Himself gives the final answer?

The Worth of a Good Life

Consider someone who has dealt honestly with others, cared for her family and helped her neighbours through difficult years. She has never claimed to be without fault. She knows occasions on which she could have acted better, and some she has never stopped regretting.

Even so, the shape of her life is plain. People trusted her because she kept her word. Someone was fed, housed or defended because she chose to help. If she asks whether any of that matters to God, it would be a poor answer to tell her that she is proud.

The help she gave remains help. The people who received it do not lose its value because a question has been raised about her standing before Christ. Her choices were real, and so were their effects. Few would dispute that. The difficulty lies in what, if anything, follows from it.

We make such distinctions every day. A court weighs what a person did and does not treat everyone before it as though their conduct were identical. A family remembers who was present during hardship. A community may honour someone who gave years of service without first demanding proof of perfection.

These judgments can be mistaken, and a public reputation may conceal much. Yet nobody believes that cruelty and kindness amount to the same thing. The difference matters, and we act on it daily.

The criminal’s welcome may trouble an upright person with no religious achievements to claim. She may not even be concerned with admission to Christ’s kingdom, but simply wonder why a just God would promise Paradise to a confessed offender while her own efforts to live honourably offer no such assurance.

We know too little of the criminal’s earlier life to compare two complete histories. What we do know is his admission of wrongdoing, and Christ’s promise gives him the future that many people hope to receive. Whatever his past, the contrast she feels is not hard to follow.

Perhaps she would put the concern more quietly. She does not demand that the criminal be shut out. She may even be glad that mercy reached him. Still, she wonders whether her own efforts to live responsibly have any bearing on how God sees her.

That is a fair question. Grace should not require us to pretend that goodness is merely a pleasant appearance concealing the same moral record in everyone. People make choices, those choices affect others, and some devote years to doing what is right at considerable personal cost.

Paul writes that God “will render to every man according to his deeds.” Romans 2:6. He goes on to say that God shows no partiality. Whatever else his argument demands, it does not treat human conduct as beneath God’s notice.

If deeds matter enough to be examined, the morally serious person is entitled to ask what they count for. The question presses harder when she has watched someone else do harm. To hear that the wrongdoer is welcome in heaven may leave her wondering whether the good she tried to do was seen with equal clarity. It is a quiet question, and it is easily mistaken for envy.

The Claim of the Faithful

The believer comes to the same question from another direction. For a Christian who has obeyed Christ for years, it weighs differently. Faithful service often rests on unseen choices, such as resisting temptation, giving time when tired, sharing money needed at home or caring for someone unable to repay it.

Some believers have held to their faith through illness, persecution or loss. They have prayed, worshipped and served while longing to be with Christ. Their hope has shaped every year of the life they lived. They were not waiting for a reward when they began, and many could not say when the habit of obedience became their own.

A person with such a history may hear the criminal’s story and ask what becomes of the years. He turns to Jesus in his final hours and receives a promise of paradise. They have followed Christ through years in which turning away would sometimes have been easier. To them the arithmetic of the years looks very uneven.

We should not accuse that person of pride for asking whether faithful years mean anything. Scripture urges obedience, and Christ speaks of doing His Father’s will. If those things matter, we ought to be able to say so without embarrassment. A believer who has spent years in obedience is not wrong to wonder whether anyone noticed.

Jesus gives voice to a related complaint in His parable of the labourers. Those who worked all day object when late arrivals receive the same payment:

“These last have wrought but one hour, and thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day.” Matthew 20:12

Anyone who has worked a long day beside someone who arrived at the end of it will recognise the complaint. The labourers are not the people at Calvary. Still, their words let us feel why an equal welcome can be hard for someone who has borne the day’s heat. They are asking whether their labour has counted.

Christian service also benefits real people. Someone taught a child, visited a prisoner, nursed the sick or gave to a person in need. Such work cannot purchase Paradise, yet no one who received it would call it worthless.

Others make a more particular appeal, and Jesus meets it Himself. The people in Matthew 7 call Jesus Lord and ask whether they have not prophesied, cast out devils and done “many wonderful works” in His name. Matthew 7:22. Their confidence rests on activities they associate directly with Him.

We know Christ’s answer: “I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” Matthew 7:23. We cannot soften it. Neither can we invent a private motive for every act they mention, or declare without examination that nothing good could have come from their activity.

Their expectation is easy to understand. Works done in Christ’s name, they assume, will carry weight with Christ. If He refuses them, the reader may fairly ask why that expectation fails.

The question sharpens when we read what Jesus has just said:

“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” Matthew 7:21

We cannot remove the second half of that sentence to make the criminal’s welcome easier to explain. Jesus speaks of doing the Father’s will, then describes people who point to work done in His name. How are we to understand the difference? For now it is enough to see that the question is real.

The Weight of Good Works

The defence does not rest on sentiment alone. Scripture gives it further force. Paul writes to believers:

“For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.” 2 Corinthians 5:10

Paul is addressing the church, and the verse does not settle every question about entry into the Kingdom of God. It does say that what believers have done will be reckoned with when they appear before Christ.

Romans says the same of God, who renders to every person according to deeds. Romans 2:6–11 places good and evil conduct before a God who judges without respect of persons. Those words challenge any easy suggestion that grace makes obedience insignificant.

The defence can therefore put its question plainly. If God commands goodness, sees what people do and judges according to works, should a good life not count in a person’s favour? If Christ calls people to do the Father’s will, should works undertaken in His name have no bearing on their appeal to Him?

A lawyer examining a person’s case may be presented with a substantial record of public service. The evidence may establish years of dedication, responsibilities faithfully discharged and countless lives improved. Such a record deserves fair consideration.

To dismiss it merely because it cannot answer every conceivable question would be unjust. The same fairness is owed to those who have lived faithfully and uprightly.

But every record must also be assessed against the question it is intended to answer. Evidence of service shows what a person has accomplished. Whether those accomplishments confer a right to a particular decision is another matter, one the record alone cannot resolve.

The distinction matters here. A person’s good works may be real. They may have relieved suffering, fulfilled a duty or honoured God. None of that is erased by asking whether the person can present them as grounds on which Christ is obliged to admit them.

The upright person asks whether God values the life she has lived. The faithful worker asks whether Christ sees years of service. Both are owed an answer before either is told what that life or service can establish.

Religious people are not the only ones who can mistake value for entitlement. One person may say, “I have never prophesied in Christ’s name, but I have tried to be decent and have done less harm than many.” Another may say, “I have served Him for years and done the work He asked me to do.” The records differ. Each still has to ask what follows from it.

The Hope of Being Received

Jesus tells a parable about a Pharisee who points to his fasting and tithing while a publican nearby asks God for mercy. Luke 18:9–14. The Pharisee and the publican are not the claimants and the criminal, but their story puts a familiar question to us. What may a person rightly expect on the strength of what he has done?

We should not wave away fasting, generosity or years of service, or suppose that every upright person secretly despises others. A good deed still benefits those who receive it, whatever questions arise about the one who did it.

The morally serious person has a case. So does the believer who served through years of difficulty. Scripture’s words about obedience and judgment according to works give both reason to ask how their conduct figures in Christ’s answer.

What remains in dispute is whether a record that earns recognition also gives its bearer a right to admission into heaven. The people in Matthew 7 believe that what they have done in Christ’s name should speak for them. Christ refuses them. Their appeal has force, and so does His answer.

The criminal has no years of faithful service to offer. He has his admission of guilt, and Christ welcomes him. Others have devoted years to living uprightly, while those in Matthew 7 present works they expect Christ to acknowledge.

It is reasonable to ask why these records appear to produce outcomes so contrary to what we might expect.

The two protests now stand together. If the criminal enters Paradise, what becomes of justice for the wrong he has committed? If even remarkable works performed in Christ’s name cannot secure entry, what becomes of deserving?

Harm matters, and years of goodness are not without value. Both protests arise from these, and both raise the question of what Christ sees when He gives His answer.

The criminal’s welcome troubles us only if mercy requires God to overlook guilt. Whether it does depends on the Man who promised him Paradise.

sections.title: Part II
sections.subtitle: The God who Admits a Criminal
sections.html:
The previous Part left us with questions that no kinder view of the criminal can answer. He admitted that his punishment was deserved. Jesus nevertheless promised him Paradise.

A criminal in heaven sounds like a contradiction, yet the promise came from Christ. His admission was no defence against his past, and Jesus did not ask him to produce one. How, then, could his welcome be just?

The concerns of those who have suffered from wrongdoing accompany us to the Cross, as do those of people whose upright conduct and faithful service deserve recognition. Neither can be dismissed. Both raise legitimate questions, and the Cross must answer them. Any answer must confront the guilt the criminal acknowledged without overlooking the lives that wrongdoing may have changed.

The question becomes especially painful for someone who has suffered at another’s hands. To learn that the offender has received mercy may deepen the hurt, particularly if forgiveness appears to set aside the wrong while leaving its consequences untouched. Such a person may accept the possibility of forgiveness and still ask whether justice has been served.

Saying that Jesus was moved by the criminal’s final words does not settle that concern. The man’s plea, however sincere, does not account for the promise he receives. His guilt stays real, whatever the nearness of death. Something other than sympathy has to carry the promise.

The answer lies with the innocent Man who made the promise, and the criminal himself points us there. He speaks of the punishment he and his companion deserve, then says of Jesus, “this man hath done nothing amiss.” Luke 23:41. His words are brief, and they carry the whole turn of the scene.

All three men are dying, but the criminal refuses to place them on the same moral footing. Jesus has done nothing to deserve His sentence. Why, then, is He at Calvary? Whatever is happening there must be more than compassion in the face of death, or His promise to the guilty man has no ground.

At the Cross, an unexpected reversal unfolds. The innocent Man is condemned alongside the guilty, and the question remains what His death means for someone with no defence to offer. Any explanation must account for the promise of Paradise without diminishing the criminal’s own admission of guilt.

The Cross may explain how mercy is possible without making its recipients any easier for us to accept. Would we welcome the same promise if we knew the offence for which the criminal was condemned? We are right to care about what he did and about anyone who suffered because of it. Grace is easy to affirm in principle, but our willingness to embrace it may be tested when we can picture the person to whom it is extended.

Scripture records other occasions when people struggled with God’s willingness to show mercy, and their reactions are easy to recognise. We want God to be just, and we have our own sense of what justice requires. When His compassion reaches someone we would have kept at a distance, we may ask whether our difficulty lies in the mercy itself or in our expectation of where it should stop. The criminal’s case tests the same instinct.

The question now turns towards us. We may have lived better than the criminal in ways that matter. But does that give us stronger grounds on which to seek God’s welcome? How we judge the man beside Jesus may reveal what we believe our own conduct deserves. This is uncomfortable territory, and we should resist the temptation to leave it too quickly.

For now, simple conclusions will not suffice. The criminal’s guilt remains significant, and concern for those he may have harmed is not something to be dismissed. Christ’s promise demands an explanation in which His mercy and God’s justice are both upheld.

The criminal himself directs our attention to where the answer lies. He looks beyond his deserved punishment to the innocent Man dying beside him. What can that Man accomplish for someone whose guilt remains undeniable?

sections.title: The Great Reversal
sections.html:
The criminal says something about the three crosses that is easy to miss:

“And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss.” Luke 23:41

He makes no claim that his sentence is mistaken. He separates his own position from that of the Man beside him. They are dying under the same public shame, though not for the same reason.

Then comes the reversal. The man who deserves his sentence receives a promise of Paradise from the Man who does not deserve His cross.

An innocent man can be condemned by a human court. His innocence would expose an injustice, but it would not explain how a guilty man could be promised Paradise. What, then, was happening at the middle Cross? What could Jesus give the criminal that the criminal could never have secured for himself?

A Cross He Did Not Deserve

A passer-by might have seen three executions. The criminal saw one man suffering who had done no wrong. Scripture asks us to look further.

Isaiah writes of the Lord’s servant:

“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” Isaiah 53:5

The wounds are His; the transgressions are ours. For Isaiah the two belong together, and the prophet will not let them be read apart. The suffering of the innocent is no sad coincidence beside other people’s wrongdoing.

The next verse makes the connection plainer:

“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.” Isaiah 53:6

Those who went astray remain responsible for their conduct, though another bears their iniquity. The promise made to the criminal begins to make sense only when both halves of that sentence are kept in view.

Peter later speaks of Christ in much the same way: “Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree.” 1 Peter 2:24

And again: “For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.” 1 Peter 3:18

“The just for the unjust” is an unsettling phrase. We cannot declare the unjust person righteous because his story moves us, nor did the just One suffer for any wrongdoing of His own. Peter explains the purpose of His suffering: “that he might bring us to God.”

We sometimes describe this as substitution. The term is useful, provided it does not replace the explanation it requires. Christ did not simply suffer alongside the guilty or offer them an example of endurance. Scripture declares that He bore sins that were not His own.
