At Calvary, this was unfolding as the criminal spoke to Him. He could see the innocent One dying beside him, but could not comprehend all that His death would accomplish. We, with the fuller testimony of Scripture, can see beyond what was visible from his cross.

Even this fuller account leaves an objection. If someone else bore the cost of the criminal’s wrongdoing, does that answer for what he had done?

The Objection That Remains

When one person commits a wrong, we do not ordinarily regard the matter as settled simply because another offers to bear its cost. The difficulty becomes greater when others have suffered as a result of the offence.

A client cannot appoint an innocent stranger to answer a charge because the arrangement suits them both. The person harmed has an interest in the matter. Justice demands an account of what happened, who bears responsibility and whether the proposed remedy adequately addresses the wrong. Those questions remain, however willingly a volunteer offers to bear the cost.

The criminal’s case calls for the same rigour. Luke does not tell us the offence for which he was condemned or identify anyone who suffered through his deeds. We must not invent a victim’s story, and we may not use the absence of details to pretend that his guilt had no consequences.

The criminal did not devise Christ’s death as a means of escaping his sentence. He admitted what he deserved, turned to Jesus and received an answer he could not demand.

Christ is no unwilling stranger made to bear another’s wrong. The Son freely gives Himself; in Him, God addresses the sin from which the guilty cannot free themselves. Jesus makes the voluntary nature of His sacrifice unmistakable:

“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.” John 10:18

That declaration alone does not settle the objection. We still need to consider whether welcoming the guilty can be reconciled with God’s justice.

Paul directs us to God’s work through Christ, declaring “the righteousness of God” “by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe.” Romans 3:21–22. The question is how the guilty criminal can stand before God, and no overlooked virtue will answer it.

Paul then writes of Christ:

“Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God; to declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.” Romans 3:25–26

Propitiation is not a word we commonly use across dinner tables. Paul connects Christ’s blood with God’s response to sin, making clear that God demonstrates His righteousness even as He justifies the person who believes in Jesus.

For Paul, mercy does not come at the expense of justice. God remains “just, and the justifier.” He upholds His righteousness even as He welcomes the guilty.

A human judge who waived a serious charge without addressing it would invite a proper challenge. A reassuring speech about compassion would not answer the person who asked what became of the wrong. Paul sends us somewhere more demanding, to Christ crucified. Only there does the question about the wrong receive an answer.

The analogy helps us see the question Paul refuses to avoid, the one any judge would raise concerning a pardon. How can God justify someone who has sinned? Paul places Christ’s costly death within the demonstration of God’s righteousness, not as an exception to it.

A person harmed by the criminal would not have found every question about his wrongdoing answered that afternoon. God’s reconciliation of a sinner to Himself does not mean that every earthly injury has been remedied. We must distinguish these matters if we are to speak truthfully about either.

Nothing Left to Offer

The criminal could admit his guilt, acknowledge Jesus’ innocence and appeal to Him. These responses matter, and Luke records them. Yet none could atone for his past. His admission did not undo his deeds, nor did his appeal entitle him to mercy. With death approaching, he had no prospect of future obedience to offer in recompense. He came to the end of his life with empty hands.

The order matters. He does not make himself acceptable and then receive a promise. He turns to the One dying beside him, and Jesus promises what the man cannot earn.

We might be tempted to give his words more power than Luke gives them. He rebukes the other criminal, admits that his sentence is just and asks Jesus to remember him. They are remarkable words from a man on a cross, and they are still the words of someone who needs mercy.

Imagine an apology offered after a grave breach of trust. It may be sincere and necessary. It may be the first time the person harmed hears the truth without excuses. Even so, it does not restore what was lost.

The criminal’s admission matters, but it does not settle his account. He can turn to Christ without minimising his wrongdoing, and acknowledging it does not make Christ’s promise his due.

Paul expresses the deeper reversal in a single sentence:

“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” 2 Corinthians 5:21

Paul does not say that Christ became personally guilty of crimes others committed. He speaks of the One who knew no sin taking the place of sinners, so that they might stand before God in Him.

Beside Jesus, the criminal acknowledges his deserved punishment; Jesus has done nothing amiss. The guilty man hears a promise of Paradise while the innocent Man remains on His cross.

That is the great reversal. Christ does not call the guilty man innocent; He bears what the man cannot bear for himself.

The Promise Only Christ Could Make

Jesus’ answer is personal and immediate: “Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” Luke 23:43

The criminal had asked to be remembered when Jesus came into His kingdom. Jesus promises more than remembrance, and He promises it sooner than the man requested. “To day.”

He also says, “with me.” Paradise is not offered as a place the criminal enters on his own after finding a favourable rule. His hope rests on the Person speaking to him.

A promise is only as good as the one who makes it. A lawyer may assure his condemned client that a stay of execution or an appeal to a higher court may still be possible, and that things will somehow turn out well. The reassurance might be kind, but its force would depend on whether the lawyer had any power to deliver what was promised.

Jesus speaks as someone able to give what He names. Elsewhere He says that the Father has given the Son authority to give life and has committed judgment to Him. John 5:21–22. At Calvary, the One who will judge speaks directly to a guilty man about his future.

The setting makes that authority difficult to recognise. Jesus appears powerless to alter anyone’s fate. His hands are nailed to a cross, and the crowd watches Him die. Why, then, should the criminal trust a promise of life from a Man facing death beside him?

Jesus declared His power to lay down His life and take it again (John 10:17–18). His resurrection vindicated the authority hidden beneath Calvary’s shame. We can see what the criminal could not. The One who promised him Paradise rose from the dead.

Charles Spurgeon described the criminal as Christ’s last companion on earth and His first at the gate of Paradise. The image catches the force of Christ’s promise. The man will be with Him.

The promise leaves no interval in which the criminal must produce the life he had no time to live. Its certainty rests on no hidden achievement and on no verdict of ours about how impressive his final words were. Jesus says, “Verily I say unto thee.”

We do not need the man’s name to feel the force of this. We know what he admitted, whom he addressed and what Jesus said in reply. The criminal could ask to be remembered; only Christ could promise, “To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.”

The Wrong Still Matters

The hardest objection is still standing at the foot of the Cross. A wrongdoer may receive mercy from God while those harmed by his conduct go on living with the consequences. The Cross must not become a reason to silence them.

If the criminal had obligations to other people, his imminent death did not make them imaginary. A promise of Paradise does not tell us that every earthly consequence of his conduct was repaired that afternoon. Scripture does not give us those facts, and we should not claim them.

Christ’s answer to guilt before God and the redress of harm suffered by others are distinct matters. Anyone hearing this account may still wonder what became of those who had to live with the consequences of the criminal’s actions. His welcome before God gives us no grounds to disregard their suffering.

God’s mercy is no casual dismissal of evil. The innocent One suffers at the centre of the scene where the guilty man receives His promise. Nothing in Scripture permits us to conclude that every earthly consequence was resolved simply because Christ welcomed the criminal.

Much about the man’s life remains unknown, and we should not speculate about what he owed to particular people. Luke gives us a scene, not a biography. But we can say with certainty what lay beyond his power. He could not undo his past, establish his own righteousness before God or secure himself a place in Paradise.

Jesus gave him a promise while bearing sin at the middle Cross. The criminal’s admission tells us why he needed mercy; Christ’s death begins to tell us how that mercy could be given.

Even when we acknowledge the cost of mercy, we may still struggle to accept the person who receives it. Why should mercy extend to this guilty man? Such reluctance predates Calvary. Jonah wrestled with the same question. When God spared a city whose wickedness He had already condemned, the prophet responded with anger.

sections.title: My Ways Are Not Your Ways
sections.html:
The middle Cross shows how Jesus could promise Paradise to a guilty man without making light of his guilt. Another question presses. Why should mercy reach this man?

We do not know what offence brought him to Calvary. We do know that he accepted his punishment as deserved. Had Luke revealed more of his past, would Christ’s promise have been harder for us to accept? And when God extends mercy to someone whose guilt is undeniable, must His judgment conform to the limits we would impose?

“My ways are not your ways” (Isaiah 55:8) can sound like an attempt to silence difficult questions. But in Isaiah, those words immediately follow God’s invitation to the wicked to abandon their ways and return to Him, with the promise that He “will abundantly pardon” (Isaiah 55:7). His higher ways are revealed here in the generosity of His mercy.

Then there is the prophet who knew God’s mercy but resented its extension to those he had been sent to warn.

Mercy for the Wrong People

God sent Jonah to Nineveh with a message of judgment:

“Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.” Jonah 1:2

Nineveh is not presented as a city whose wickedness has been misunderstood. Its wrongdoing is the reason why Jonah is sent. God sees the evil before He sends a warning, and nothing about the city’s conduct escapes His notice.

Jonah eventually obeys, and the people respond. The king calls on them to turn from their evil ways and from “the violence that is in their hands” (Jonah 3:8). Their wrongdoing is not left concealed nor minimised, and the change required of them is equally clear.

Then the account tells us:

“And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.” Jonah 3:10

In that last clause, “the evil” is the calamity God had threatened, not a wrong He intended to commit. He saw their turning and did not bring the threatened destruction upon the city.

Jonah’s reaction is striking. “But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry.” Jonah 4:1

He had not misunderstood God’s character. He explains why he fled from God’s instructions in the first place:

“For I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil.” Jonah 4:2

Jonah knew God might show mercy. That was the problem.

Nineveh’s violence was real, and Jonah’s anger is not difficult to understand. A warning followed by mercy might appear to offer an unacceptable escape from consequences, particularly to someone who feared the city or knew the harm its people had caused. Scripture does not tell us that Jonah personally suffered from Nineveh’s violence, and we should not invent a history the account does not provide. Nevertheless, we can recognise the force of his objection.

Matthew Henry observed the painful turn in the account. Nineveh’s repentance brings relief to the city, while the prophet who warned it grieves to see it spared. Jonah could describe God’s mercy accurately and still object to its exercise.

God does not silence Jonah with a general declaration of divine authority. Instead, He asks whether his anger is justified. He then directs the prophet’s attention to a plant whose shade had brought him comfort.

When the plant withers, Jonah mourns its loss. God responds:

“Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night: And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?” (Jonah 4:10–11).

Jonah grieved the loss of something that had sheltered him. God invites him to consider the lives of those within the city. His question does not excuse Nineveh’s violence, for its wickedness had already been condemned. It challenges Jonah to see beyond the destruction he had anticipated.

The book ends with God’s question unanswered. Scripture does not record Jonah’s reply. Instead, the question remains before us, inviting us to consider how we ourselves would answer.

More Than Their Past

God saw both Nineveh’s wickedness and its response to His warning. His mercy did not require a favourable account of the city’s past. The wrongdoing was condemned, and the people were called to turn from it. Mercy was extended because the city turned from the evil for which they had been condemned.

Consider Jonah’s account alongside that of the criminal. Nineveh was spared a threatened judgment when its people turned from their wickedness. The criminal received the promise of Paradise as he faced death. The circumstances differ, and neither account fully explains the other.

Both accounts confront us with a similar difficulty. Undeniable wrongdoing is met with mercy, and those who witness it may struggle to accept the outcome. The question is whether the wrongdoer can still be welcomed.

If asked whether the criminal’s deeds mattered, we could answer without hesitation. He himself acknowledged that his punishment was deserved. The difficulty arises when we presume that his guilt must place him beyond the reach of God’s mercy.

I understand the impulse. In legal practice, one may accept that mercy has a principled basis and still struggle to see it granted to someone who has caused serious harm. Knowledge of a case can sharpen that discomfort. The facts do not become less painful because the decision has a sound basis.

There are also decisions we must continue to make for the protection of others. Before entrusting someone with funds or giving them responsibility for a vulnerable person, a record of conduct matters. A person who has been forgiven may still have debts to pay, trust to rebuild or legal consequences to face.

God does not require us to disregard these distinctions. Mercy must never come at the expense of another’s safety, and a person’s fitness for responsibility is a different question from whether God may forgive him. An answer to one does not resolve the other.

Those who have suffered may fear that forgiveness will be used to demand their trust, reconciliation or silence. Jonah’s account and Christ’s promise to the criminal impose no such obligations. God’s mercy does not remove the need to address those matters with fairness and regard for everyone concerned.

Their suffering remains real, and their losses cannot be dismissed. What remains is whether those losses establish a boundary beyond which God may not extend His mercy.

The Sentence We Often Shorten

God speaks through Isaiah:

“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.” Isaiah 55:8–9

These verses are often used to say that God knows things we do not. That is true, but starting at verse eight can cause us to miss the thought that has just been expressed. The verses before them change what they mean.

The passage calls people to seek the Lord and turn to Him:

“Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.” Isaiah 55:7

Isaiah proclaims a mercy more generous than the returning sinner might dare to hope for, or an observer might be willing to accept.

The word “abundantly” is significant. We may suppose that God will pardon only a tolerable measure of wrongdoing, provided a person’s good conduct still outweighs the bad. But Isaiah speaks to the wicked, promising a pardon sufficient for those who turn to the Lord, however grave their past.

The invitation is addressed to those who have sinful ways to forsake, and is not reserved for people who can demonstrate that they have needed little forgiveness. God offers mercy without requiring a favourable account of their past.

Pardon is not something anyone can claim as a right. The person who returns to God cannot prescribe its terms or demand credit for changing course. He comes in response to God’s invitation, trusting His promise that He “will have mercy upon him.”

This offers no licence to continue in wrongdoing. The wicked are called to forsake their ways. God’s willingness to forgive does not imply approval of the conduct He commands them to abandon.

At Calvary, the criminal had scarcely any time left to demonstrate a changed life. We cannot invent years of obedience he never lived, and we cannot disregard the response Luke records. He acknowledged the justice of his punishment, recognised Jesus’ innocence and appealed to Him for mercy.

Isaiah and Luke present different circumstances, but together they challenge a familiar assumption: that the weight of a person’s past determines the limits of God’s willingness to receive those who turn to Him.

The Limits of Our Judgment

Luke tells us what the criminal said and what Jesus answered. He does not give us a full account of the man’s past or of every movement within his heart. We would overreach if we used those silences to make him more deserving or more blameworthy than the account permits.

Suppose his offence had been recorded in detail. Some readers might then find Christ’s promise harder to receive once they could picture those affected because of it. Others might search for something in the man’s earlier life that would make him more deserving of sympathy.

The desire to know more is understandable. Sometimes, however, we seek further details because we wish to judge for ourselves, with greater certainty, whether Christ ought to have welcome him. Jonah’s reaction reminds us how readily we may assume that such a judgment belongs to us.

None of this silences the objections. Someone who has suffered may ask hard questions about mercy because the harm remains part of daily life. Another person may fear that talk of forgiveness will be used to excuse further wrongdoing. Both are owed more than a rebuke for failing to understand God’s ways.

There is humility in recognising the limit of what we know. We keep caring about the wrong. We ask whether our knowledge, even when it is substantial, gives us the authority to set the final reach of God’s mercy.

Jonah first regarded Nineveh as a city marked for judgment, and then as one that had escaped it. But God’s final question directs his attention to the people who lived within its walls. It leaves in place those who may have suffered from Nineveh's voilence, which the king acknowledged when he called the city to repentance.

Not everyone in Nineveh bore responsibility for every wrong associated with it. God calls Jonah to consider the lives of people he had come to view chiefly through the judgment he expected. His question broadens the prophet’s perspective without requiring him to overlook the city’s wickedness.

The same restraint applies to the man at Calvary. We do not know who may have suffered because of him, and Christ’s promise does not tell such a person what to feel. It does show that Jesus could hear the criminal’s admission clearly and still address him with mercy.

We do not need to force these concerns into an easy settlement. The Cross tells us that God’s answer to sin is costly. Isaiah says that He will “abundantly pardon” those who turn to Him. Jonah shows a prophet who knew God’s character and still struggled when its mercy reached Nineveh.

A Question Turned Towards Us

We can understand Jonah’s anger while recognising the danger within it. That is what makes his story instructive. He saw Nineveh’s wickedness clear, but struggled to accept God’s willingness to show mercy when the city repented. His anger arose from knowing precisely how merciful God could be.

We may encounter the same difficulty in less obvious ways. We do not openly declare our opposition to grace. Instead, we insist that a person has gone too far, that the record of wrongdoing should settle the question, or that welcoming such a sinner would send the wrong message.

At times, such concerns arise from a legitimate desire to protect others. At other times, they conceal a belief that we stand on firmer ground before God than those whose wrongdoing is more apparent. We must learn to distinguish between the two, even when doing so requires uncomfortable honesty about ourselves.

The criminal at Calvary leaves us with no comfortable reason to regard him as an easy recipient of mercy. Isaiah gives us words we might hesitate to apply to him. God “will abundantly pardon.” Jonah asks whether we can still welcome those words when God’s mercy reaches someone we would have excluded.

That question has a way of turning towards the person who asks it. We may have lived better than the criminal without acquiring a stronger claim before God. Jesus told a parable about two men who went to pray, and it speaks directly to the danger of such comparisons.

sections.title: Part III
sections.subtitle: When Deserving Becomes Entitlement
sections.html:
The criminal could point to no work that might explain Christ’s promise. The people who address Jesus as “Lord, Lord” present the opposite case. They speak of remarkable works done in His name and expect Him to receive them.

Religious achievement is only one way we come to believe we deserve God’s welcome. A person may have no ministry to describe and still point to a life spent acting decently, helping others and avoiding serious harm. If Christ promises Paradise to a condemned criminal, she may reasonably ask whether her conduct counts for anything. It is a question people ask quietly, and usually alone.

Between those two cases sits a sharper question. When does believing that goodness matters become believing that it entitles us to God’s welcome into heaven?

The change is easy to miss, because its starting points are sound. We ought to recognise faithful conduct and the people it has helped. We ought also to distinguish someone who has tried to live well from someone whose wrongdoing is plain. Those judgments serve real purposes in ordinary life, and Scripture itself speaks plainly of what people do.

Comparison can begin to do more than help us recognise a difference. We may look at another person’s failures and conclude that our own record must place us on firmer ground before God. We may even find reassurance in the thought that, whatever else could be said about us, we are not like that person.

Jesus tells a story about two men at prayer that brings this confidence into view. One gives an account of his religious conduct and distinguishes himself from people he considers worse. The other asks for mercy. Whatever good the first man has done stays good, even though he relies on it for more than it can establish.

Religious confidence grows in a similar way, though its record looks different. The people in Christ’s warning say more than that they have avoided wrongdoing. They call Him Lord and point to prophecy, casting out devils and “many wonderful works” done in His name. Matthew 7:22. Their appeal has weight.

If someone had done such things, we would want to know what happened. We might admire what we saw and regard it as evidence of a life devoted to Christ. The people helped by an act would have reason to value the help, even if a further question remained about the person who performed it.

Jesus says that people who bring Him this account will hear words they did not expect. “I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” Matthew 7:23. We cannot soften His answer by declaring, without evidence, that every work they mention was false or that nothing they did could have benefited anyone. Whatever else they felt, they were surprised.

To regard every decent person as secretly proud would not answer the question. Moral and religious lives differ, and the good accomplished through them matters. A good deed remains a good deed. The issue is what happens when someone moves from believing that such deeds matter to assuming that they establish a claim to Christ’s welcome.

That transition is more subtle than it appears. What does comparison with another person establish about our standing before God? What do works performed in Christ’s name demonstrate, and what questions might they leave unresolved? When Jesus speaks of doing His Father’s will, how are we to understand that alongside His rejection of those who expected their works to secure His approval?

We must confront the warning without evasion or prejudice. It would be convenient to confine Christ’s words to obvious impostors or members of another church. But we have no grounds for doing so, nor may we use their rejection to cast suspicion upon everyone engaged in ministry, any more than we may use the criminal’s welcome to diminish a lifetime of obedience.

Decent conduct and faithful service have genuine value. The question is whether that value establishes a claim upon God. A subtler form of confidence begins with the assumption that, when measured against someone whose failures are evident, our own lives must speak sufficiently well in our favour.

sections.title: The High Moral Horse
sections.html:
It is possible to object to mercy for the criminal without believing we have earned Paradise ourselves. We may simply think that we have lived better than he did. Perhaps we have. The question is what that difference establishes before God.

Jesus told a parable to people who were confident of their own standing and looked down on others:

“And he spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others.” Luke 18:9

Their confidence and their contempt belong together. The faults of other people help them feel secure about themselves. From that height, the criminal at Calvary is easy to judge.

We are right to distinguish integrity from deceit and kindness from cruelty. Jesus does not ask us to pretend those differences disappear. He asks what happens when we turn them into a claim that God should receive us because we stand above someone else.

The First Prayer and Its Comparison

Jesus begins:

“Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican.” Luke 18:10

They come to the same place and, outwardly, for the same purpose. Each is about to speak to God. Jesus lets us hear the Pharisee first:

“The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.

I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.” Luke 18:11–12

We should listen before rushing to condemn him. Extortion, injustice and adultery are serious wrongs. Fasting and giving may be sincere acts of devotion. If he has avoided the first and practised the second, his conduct differs in important ways from that of someone who has not.

Such differences matter to other people. A person who does not extort is safer to deal with than one who does. Faithfulness protects a marriage. Generosity can meet a need. The parable does not require us to call those goods worthless.

The Pharisee begins with thanks to God. We should notice that too. His error cannot be explained simply by saying that he forgot to mention God or falsely claimed to have accomplished everything alone.

Augustine drew attention to this aspect of the prayer. The Pharisee thanked God for what he possessed, but spoke as though his righteousness lacked nothing. He also measured himself favourably against the publican. It is possible to acknowledge God’s help while approaching Him with the confidence that one’s own account is already sufficient.

Luke says the Pharisee “prayed thus with himself.” Though he addresses God, his attention remains fixed on his own conduct and the conduct of others. His words contain thanks, but they give us little sense that he has come needing anything from the One to whom he speaks.

He lists what he avoids, what he does and the people from whom he believes he is different. Then he brings another worshipper into his argument with the words “even as this publican.”

The publican has come to pray. In the Pharisee’s account, however, he becomes useful as someone beneath him. Whatever else the Pharisee knows about this man, the comparison makes his own position appear secure.

This is a familiar human tendency. We may judge our conduct by comparing it with the worst behaviour around us. Such comparisons can offer reassurance, especially when our own shortcomings are less apparent.

Suppose I am asked to advise a client facing a legal claim. The client arrives with a substantial file documenting misconduct by a competitor, much of it considerably worse than anything alleged against them. The evidence may be accurate and relevant to another enquiry. But if the issue is whether my client breached a particular obligation, the competitor’s wrongdoing does not resolve that question.

The Pharisee’s comparison suffers from a similar weakness. He may well have avoided offences of which the publican was guilty. Jesus does not suggest that every claim in his prayer was untrue. Nevertheless, the publican’s conduct could not establish that the Pharisee himself stood before God without need of mercy.

Moral distinctions remain legitimate. The trouble comes when another person’s failures become part of the grounds upon which we claim acceptance before God.

We need not speak like the Pharisee to share his disposition. “At least I have never done that” may express a valid distinction in conduct. But it becomes precarious when presented as our answer before God.

Consider how readily the standard moves. We compare ourselves with someone whose dishonesty is public, but seldom ask whether the people we have disappointed would give the same account of our integrity that we give ourselves. We may be accurate about the other person and still too generous in our assessment of our own conduct.

Nor is the problem confined to people who are outwardly strict or religious. A person proud of being less judgmental, kinder or more generous than a neighbour can make the same comparison. The high moral horse can be ridden in several styles.

Jesus does not leave us to infer the publican’s response. He gives the second man his own voice.

The Other Prayer

“And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.” Luke 18:13

He does not offer a competing list. He does not claim that the Pharisee’s faults cancel his own. He asks for mercy.

His posture does not earn God’s approval. A person can lower his eyes without admitting any wrong at all. Jesus presents a man who admits his sin and asks God for mercy.

That appeal resembles the criminal’s in a significant respect. The criminal says that his sentence is deserved and asks Jesus to remember him. The publican asks God to be merciful to him, a sinner. Neither tries to make another person’s record the ground of his own acceptance.

Their circumstances differ. One faces death at Calvary; the other enters the temple to pray. Jesus does not equate their stories but allows each man to speak for himself.

The publican may have wronged people who are nowhere in the temple scene. Asking for mercy does not make any injury imaginary, nor does it show us what he might need to put right. Jesus gives us enough to hear his prayer without supplying a complete history of his conduct.

Then He gives a verdict we might not have expected:

“I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.” Luke 18:14

The publican returns home justified. The man who could recite his religious duties does not receive the same verdict. Jesus is telling us how each man stood at the end of his prayer, not merely which prayer sounded better.

He also tells us why the outcome is so surprising. The man who elevated himself over another is brought low. The one who acknowledged his need is raised. That is the reversal Jesus places before His hearers.

The publican did not come to the temple with humility as a new achievement to set against the Pharisee’s fasting and giving. He came asking for mercy. If we turn his lowered eyes into a superior religious performance, we have found another way to make the Pharisee’s mistake.

The Difference We Must Preserve

We could mishandle this story by treating the Pharisee’s avoidance of wrongdoing as though it had no value. We could also treat the publican’s appeal for mercy as though it proved that his conduct had harmed no one.

Jesus asks us to make neither mistake. His verdict concerns how the men came before God. The Pharisee relied upon his conduct and a comparison with another person. The publican sought mercy as a sinner.

If the publican had wronged someone, that person’s claim would still matter. The parable does not tell us his full history or what he might owe. We need not invent either in order to hear Jesus’ verdict.

The Pharisee, for his part, need not have committed the publican’s offences in order to need mercy. We miss the force of the parable if we secretly rewrite him as a man whose every claim about his conduct is a lie. Jesus’ point is more unsettling when we allow that his good conduct may be exactly what he says it is.

He has brought valid distinctions to the wrong question. He asks them to do what they cannot, which is to establish his righteousness before God by placing him above another sinner.

Paul later puts the wider human difficulty plainly:

“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” Romans 3:23

“All” covers people who have done very different wrongs and caused very different harm. None of us can settle our standing before God by finding a person whose record is worse.

Many have lived more responsibly than the criminal, protecting families, keeping promises and sparing others harm. The question is whether those differences give them a claim on Paradise he lacked.

Jesus’ parable cautions us against reaching conclusions too readily. A comparison may accurately distinguish one person’s conduct from another’s while giving us false confidence about our standing before God. The Pharisee recognised wrongdoing in others. His error was to approach God as though he himself had no need of mercy.

The lesson reaches into ordinary life. If a neighbour has cheated someone, our claim to have dealt honestly may be both true and significant. If a friend has neglected a responsibility we faithfully discharged, that distinction may matter to everyone concerned. We need not abandon such judgments to understand the parable.

But we must examine what follows from them. Does another person’s failure establish that we have no need of God’s mercy? Does having lived better in certain respects entitle us to the welcome that Christ alone can give?

The Pharisee answers these questions without asking them aloud. He stands before God confident in his own record, measuring himself against the publican. Jesus’ verdict reveals that the comparison could not establish what the Pharisee believed it proved.

Before We Judge

The high moral horse offers an attractive view. From it, the criminal at Calvary looks especially guilty. So does the publican. We can see their faults without much effort.

We can abandon that confidence without ceasing to take wrongdoing seriously. Instead, we should direct the same enquiry towards ourselves. What will we bring before God, and what do we expect our own record to establish?

Jesus presents two men praying in the temple. One recounts his good conduct and compares himself favourably with the other. The second simply acknowledges his need for mercy. Jesus declares that it is this man who returns home justified.

Obedience matters, but measuring ourselves against others offers uncertain grounds for hope. We may indeed have lived better than another, with consequences that matter in this life. Yet such comparisons cannot establish our standing before God.

The criminal’s welcome required us to consider the Man who made the promise, the abundance of God’s pardon and the position from which we judge its recipients. The Pharisee’s prayer introduces a caution. Even genuine differences in conduct cannot turn another person’s failures into grounds for our acceptance before God.

But this leaves unresolved the other answer with which our investigation began. Those who cry “Lord, Lord” do not point to the criminal and insist that they lived better than he did. They appeal instead to works performed in Christ’s own name. That claim deserves an examination of its own.

sections.title: Many Wonderful Works
sections.html:
Good works remain good. The hungry should be fed, neighbours in distress should be helped, and promises should be honoured. Christ’s warning against placing confidence in our works is no reason to neglect them.

The people Jesus describes expect Him to acknowledge their service. They speak of prophecy, casting out devils and performing many works in His name. Their appeal rests on what they claim to have accomplished and what they expect Christ to make of it.

Three questions must be distinguished. What do these people claim to have done? Might others have benefited from their works? And would such benefits establish what they believe those works prove about their standing before Christ?

Jesus reports their words:

“Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?” Matthew 7:22

They repeat “in thy name” with each claim, confident that the works performed under Jesus’ authority will count in their favour when He considers their case.

An Impressive Record

Jesus tells us what the claimants will say. He does not give us an independent account of each prophecy, deliverance or wonderful work. We cannot say that every event happened exactly as they describe it.

Assuming that none of the claimed works occurred does not settle the difficulty. Jesus lets their appeal stand before He answers. We should hear its full force, knowing that the welcome they expect will not come.

Each claim is impressive on its face. Prophecy invokes Christ’s authority. Casting out devils would be memorable if it occurred as described. “Many wonderful works” is what the claimants regard as a sustained record, not one remarkable event.

Matthew does not tell us how others responded to that activity. Some might have welcomed it; others might have raised questions. We cannot call witnesses the passage has not supplied or assume what they would have said.

We can, however, understand the claimants’ confidence. They cite things they say they did in His name and expect Him to recognise those works when He decides whether to receive them.

Immediately before reporting their appeal, Jesus has said:

“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” Matthew 7:21

The people in the next verse offer more than a profession of loyalty. They point to what they say they have done in Jesus’ name. Does that work answer His call to do the Father’s will?

Christ has named the Father’s will before He lets us hear their list. The list cannot tell us whether it meets that will. We must wait for His response.

Good Done for Others

A person may benefit from an act even when serious questions remain about the one who performed it. Food given to a hungry child meets a real need. Help offered to a family during illness can matter greatly to them, whatever we later learn about the helper.

Hold that distinction in view when reading Matthew 7. Christ’s refusal is not a verdict on whether others benefited. Matthew does not tell us what happened in each instance or how those involved understood what they had seen.

The distinction matters in ordinary Christian service. A school may be supported, a debt paid or a family helped through a difficult season. Those who received the help need not question its value because someone later asks what the work says about the person who undertook it.

I encounter this responsibility in the work of a foundation. School support must reach the children it is meant to help. Literature offered freely should reach readers who can use it. A community project should be judged, in part, by whether it meets the need for which it was undertaken.

Beneficiaries are owed a plain account of that work, and so are those who give their resources. These are questions about real people and real outcomes. They remain important when we turn to the organiser’s spiritual life.

A completed project can usually be inspected. Matthew gives us no comparable detail by which to assess each extraordinary act the claimants mention. The example makes a narrower point. Even if others benefited, that benefit cannot settle the doer’s standing before Christ.

The question concerns me as much as anyone involved. Once the work is accounted for and its benefits acknowledged, what do I believe it establishes about me? Those who received help may rightly commend it, but they cannot answer that question on Christ’s behalf.

Paul makes the distinction unusually sharp. In a passage that speaks of remarkable gifts and costly acts, he imagines someone giving away all his goods while lacking charity. For that person, Paul says, the giving “profiteth me nothing.” 1 Corinthians 13:3

The recipients may still have received what they needed. Paul does not say the food ceased to nourish them or the gift ceased to be useful. He asks what the act profits the giver when charity is absent.

Those helped may rightly be grateful. Their gratitude cannot, on its own, establish what the giver hopes his work will count for before Christ.

The Desire to Be Seen

Jesus does not teach that good works must never be visible. Earlier in the Sermon on the Mount, He says:

“Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.” Matthew 5:16

A chapter later, He warns against giving “to be seen of them.” Matthew 6:1. People see the work in both passages. The difference lies in what the giver seeks from being seen.

Augustine addressed the apparent tension between these sayings. He observed that Christ permits the good work to be seen so that people may glorify the Father, while warning against making one’s own recognition the purpose of being seen.

That distinction matters when a charitable project must be reported publicly. Donors may need to see how money was spent. A community may need to know that a promised project was completed. An accurate report can also encourage support for further work.

The report may bring praise to those who carried out the project. Praise is pleasant, and it does not prove that their work was insincere. It does raise a question. Has the wish to be noticed begun to influence what they do, or how they tell the story, more than the needs of those they serve?

I recognise how the meaning of good works can change as a person grows older. As a younger man with few resources and fewer responsibilities, I was more likely to think about sparing money for a trip to the cinema or buying a new pair of sneakers than about funding a community project. Greater means and greater responsibility have since made it possible, and necessary, to think beyond my own immediate wants.

Abraham Maslow’s account of human needs helps explain another part of that change. As people seek security, belonging, esteem and a sense that their lives have fulfilled some purpose, service can become very important to them. That need not diminish the service. A school still benefits from support, and a community still benefits from a project completed.

Still, esteem can attach itself quietly to the work. An award, a title or public thanks may begin as recognition of something worthwhile. Over time, a person may start to value the recognition almost as much as the good accomplished.

An honour may be deserved. The question I must ask myself is whether I would still want the work done if another person’s name appeared on the plaque.

Privacy supplies no automatic answer either. A gift may be made quietly while its giver still returns to the memory of his generosity with personal satisfaction. Being unseen by others does not prevent us from admiring ourselves.

We cannot inspect a stranger’s photograph or donation and pronounce confidently upon his motives. We know too little. We know much more about our own choices.

Jesus’ warning about being seen invites that examination. The people in Matthew 7 take us a step further. Even if we knew nothing about whether they sought public praise, we would still have to hear the account they bring to Christ.

The Account We Keep for Ourselves

The danger in Matthew 7 goes past the desire for applause. The claimants are asking Christ, not a crowd, to take account of what they say they have done.

“Have we not…?” expects an answer. They name works they believe He should recognise and repeat the name in which they say those works were performed. Whether other people praised them has become secondary. What matters now is the conclusion they expect Christ to draw.

Faithful service is worth acknowledging. Someone who has given years to a church or cared for others at real personal cost may rightly hope that the work has not gone unnoticed.

But another expectation may form without ever being expressed. A person may quietly reflect on the sacrifices made for his family, the needs he met and the responsibilities he carried when others could not. All of it may deserve gratitude. But what has he come to believe it establishes before Christ?

With time, he may begin to reason, After all I have done, surely Christ must receive me. His service may remain genuinely valuable. What has changed is the significance he attaches to it. He has begun to treat his good works as grounds on which Christ ought to welcome him.

No audience is needed for that to happen. He may keep a private account, adding each sacrifice and good deed until the record he has never shown anyone becomes the one in which he places his deepest confidence.

That is what the words “good works are not enough” mean. The works may be good and the gratitude deserved, yet neither is the ground on which the giver stands before Christ.

The claimants offer a more striking account than most of us could present. They name remarkable works and say each was done in Jesus’ name.

At Calvary, a man who admitted his guilt heard a promise of Paradise. Here, people who expect their works to speak for them await an answer from the same Christ.

Then Jesus answers:

“And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” Matthew 7:23

sections.title: Part IV
sections.subtitle: Beyond Our Reckoning
sections.html:
We have considered two verdicts that challenge our understanding of justice and deserving. A condemned man receives Christ’s promise of Paradise, while those who invoke His name and appeal to their religious works hear His refusal: “I never knew you.” Matthew 7:23

This is where our reckoning begins to fail us. We understand why wrongdoing matters and why service deserves recognition. Such judgments help us protect others, honour obligations and give credit where it is due. But when we apply them to the question of whom Christ will receive, the criminal and the claimants confront us with outcomes that defy the conclusions we expected to draw.

Consider the criminal alone, and we may wonder whether mercy has come at the expense of justice. Consider the claimants alone, and we may question whether obedience and service have counted for nothing. Heard together, Christ's answers confront us with a more troubling question. Have we misunderstood what either record can establish before Him?

The difficulty is easily softened by explanations that resolve one question while neglecting another. We can speak of grace until the criminal’s guilt seems insignificant, or emphasise the limits of human merit until obedience appears pointless. Neither approach does justice to the accounts before us. Christ’s answers demand a more careful understanding of mercy, righteousness and the place of human conduct in God’s judgment.

The question of the basis on which anyone is received into His Kingdom has accompanied us from the beginning of this book. It now carries the weight of both encounters. Any answer must account for the criminal’s welcome and the claimants’ rejection. It must also explain why Jesus speaks of doing His Father’s will and why Scripture teaches that judgment will be according to works.

Another difficulty remains, concerning the life that follows the promise of grace. The criminal had scarcely any time left after Christ spoke to him. Most of us have been given longer. We have made choices, discharged responsibilities, neglected some and returned to others. If good works cannot earn God’s welcome, what place should they occupy in a life granted years to mature in faith?

Anyone tempted to use the criminal’s final hour as an excuse to postpone facing his own conduct should ask that question. So should the faithful person who fears that receiving grace empties years of obedience of their value. The criminal’s lack of time answers neither concern. What does grace produce when time is given?

So far, we have been able to examine other people. We have heard the criminal’s plea, listened to the Pharisee pray and considered the works claimed by those who asked, “Have we not…?” It is easier to recognise misplaced confidence when someone else is placing it.

The enquiry cannot end with our assessment of them. I must ask whether I have reserved a more favourable reading for my own life. The reader may find the same question waiting.

What do we expect to speak for us when Christ gives His answer? We may point to good we have done, or ask Him to take account of burdens faithfully borne. We may also know of wrongs we would rather leave outside the record.

The criminal has been in the dock long enough. It is almost time for us to take his place.

sections.title: The Injustice of It All
sections.html:
A man admits that his punishment is deserved, and Jesus promises him Paradise. Others point to “many wonderful works” done in His name, and Jesus says, “I never knew you.” (Matthew 7:22–23)

Had we been asked to judge by the records before us, would we have arrived at either verdict? The guilty man receives a promise his conduct cannot justify. The claimants are denied the welcome they believed their service would secure. What becomes of justice in the first case, and what becomes of deserving in the second?

Until now, we have considered these questions separately. Here, they meet. Can the judgments we rightly make about wrongdoing and service explain both of Christ’s answers?

The Justice We Expect

We expect conduct to have consequences. A person harmed by wrongdoing may ask for restitution, or at least for the injury to be acknowledged. A person who has served others faithfully may expect the work to be recognised.

These are reasonable expectations. We cannot live well together by treating a broken promise as though it were kept, or years of care as though no care was given. Much of law depends on making such distinctions fairly.

The difficulty begins when we expect those distinctions to decide every further question. Suppose a file contains evidence of both an offence and a long record of public service. A court may need to consider each for a particular purpose. Service rendered elsewhere does not cancel the offence. Proof of the offence does not erase the service.

We understand this in ordinary life, but we are drawn to a simpler reckoning when we place the criminal and the claimants beside each other. One admits guilt. The others cite work done in Christ’s name. Surely, we think, the better record should lead to the better answer.

The reasoning has merit. If I were deciding whom to entrust with another person’s money, an admitted offence would be relevant. If I were determining whom to honour for years of service, the work accomplished would matter. Anyone affected by either decision would be entitled to ask whether I had examined the record.

But those decisions concern particular questions. We know what is being entrusted, what loss was suffered or what service was rendered. When we ask who enters Christ’s Kingdom, are we deciding any of those matters? Or have we assumed that a record sufficient to answer them must also determine who deserves His welcome?

The record matters. Scripture declares that God will judge each person according to their deeds and that believers must appear before Christ’s judgment seat (Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10). Neither the victim’s suffering nor the beneficiary’s gratitude can be disregarded.

But these facts do not explain Christ’s two answers by themselves. Indeed, the more seriously we consider them, the more difficult those answers become to reconcile with our expectations.

The Protest on Both Sides

Imagine the person wounded by wrongdoing hearing that the offender has been promised Paradise. She may say, “I know he admitted what he did. I heard that Jesus received him. But I still bear the loss. What became of justice for me?”

The promise does not require her to deny the injury. Christ’s welcome neither settles the debt nor removes its earthly consequences. Her grievance remains legitimate.

Now let the conscientious worker speak. “I gave years to duties I could have neglected. People depended upon me, and I did not abandon them. If those years matter, why do works done even in Christ’s name fail to secure a welcome?”

The people he served did receive something, and their gratitude may be well founded. Scripture’s words about obedience and judgment according to works give the worker further reason to ask how service figures in Christ’s answer.

The protests become harder when each person hears what we say to the other. Tell the injured person that good works should count, and she may agree, but good done elsewhere does not answer her injury. Tell the worker that guilt has been dealt with at the Cross, and he may agree, but he can still ask why a guilty man is promised Paradise while workers are refused.

Say that the criminal turned to Christ, and the worker may ask why Jesus speaks so plainly about doing the Father’s will. Say that obedience decides the matter, and the injured person may ask what years of obedience the criminal had left to give.

That difference in time matters. The criminal died with no opportunity to build a later record. Others have lived for decades, making choices and carrying obligations. If we require a visible lifetime of obedience to explain welcome, the criminal’s promise unsettles us. If we say those years have no bearing at all, we must explain why Scripture treats them seriously.

We cannot escape by making faith an invisible exception whenever conduct troubles us. The man at Calvary did turn to Jesus; Luke lets us hear him do so. But if the word faith is used to prevent any question about how people live, Christ’s warnings lose their force. If works are made the answer instead, the criminal’s welcome becomes inexplicable on the record he had time to make.

We might wish that one side would yield. The injured person could be told to accept that mercy is greater than justice. The worker could be told that service was never important. Neither answer is faithful to what we have heard. God’s pardon is not indifference to harm, and Christ’s refusal does not turn the help given into an illusion.

Deciding which person deserves our sympathy will not resolve the two protests. Both ask us to take conduct seriously, and each shows what is missing from any easy explanation of the other verdict.

When Our Reckoning Fails

The most obvious calculation is to rank the two records. Put admitted guilt below remarkable service, then expect Christ’s answers to follow that order. They do not.

We might try to repair the calculation by adding and subtracting. Earlier goodness might offset wrongdoing, or many works might add up to a right to be received. But no quantity of help given to others makes a particular injury unreal. And Jesus’ answer to the claimants prevents us from treating even “many wonderful works” as a sum that compels His welcome.

Perhaps, then, the criminal is simply an exception. His life was almost over, so Christ received him by mercy; the rest of us can still rely on our better records. That lets us admire the promise while protecting the confidence we brought to the enquiry. It leaves the claimants’ refusal unanswered.

Or perhaps the claimants’ record was entirely false. If no work occurred and no one was helped, their refusal would be easier to understand. Matthew does not give us the evidence to make that declaration. Jesus reports their plea, then speaks His answer. We cannot invent facts to bring the case within our preferred calculation.

Christ’s answer must be heard in full.

“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” Matthew 7:23

“I never knew you” denies the recognition they expected. “Ye that work iniquity” reveals that their wonderful works did not tell the whole story. Christ’s judgment is clear, though Scripture does not disclose the personal history of each claimant.

Matthew Henry observes that the Christ who speaks of doing the Father’s will is the same One who answers the claimants. He observes that a person may possess gifts for ministry and even achieve apparent success without those accomplishments securing Christ’s welcome. This allows us to acknowledge the significance of their works without diminishing the force of His verdict.

Neither Henry nor we can say more about these particular speakers than Matthew does. Christ calls them workers of iniquity, and we do not soften His words. Matthew has not supplied the individual offences or motives we might find convenient to attribute to them.

The criminal’s case resists our adjustment in the opposite direction. We cannot make him innocent to justify the promise; he has admitted his guilt. His final appeal cannot be turned into a deed that earned Paradise either. It was addressed to Jesus because the man could not give himself what he asked for.

Every attempt to resolve the difficulty, whether by ranking, balancing or making exceptions, leaves something unanswered, either in what Christ has said or in what human beings have suffered or accomplished.

This is the apparent injustice that confronts us. We acknowledge the criminal’s guilt but cannot declare him excluded from Paradise, because Christ promised him a place there. We recognise whatever value the claimants’ works possessed but cannot declare them accepted, because Christ refused them. Scripture speaks of judgment according to deeds, but neither verdict can be explained by the deeds placed before us.

That limitation neither diminishes the reality of wrongdoing nor denies the value of faithful service. The guilt we can establish and the good we can acknowledge do not, by themselves, fully explain Christ’s answers. For all our careful reckoning, the verdicts remain beyond our power to pronounce.

That leaves one question.

If neither a guilty past nor an impressive record supplies the basis for entry, on what grounds does Christ admit a person to Paradise, and what does He recognise that our reckoning has missed?

sections.title: What, Then, Is the Criterion?
sections.html:
To understand why human conduct cannot, by itself, secure acceptance before God, we must examine what Scripture says about the basis of salvation and the place of good works within it.

Paul provides the answer, but we must consider his entire statement and the one that follows:

“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” Ephesians 2:8–10

The order is significant. Salvation is by grace, through faith, and is God’s gift. Those who receive it are then described as created in Christ for good works. Paul establishes the basis of salvation before describing the life that proceeds from it.

The Ground for Welcome

The criminal did not make a case that his sentence was unjust. He asked Jesus to remember him, and Jesus promised him Paradise. The promise rested on Christ, and the man had no hidden record to produce.

Paul says that sinners are “justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” Romans 3:24. He goes on to speak of God as “just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus.” Romans 3:26. The welcome is free to the sinner, and it rests on what Christ has done. God does not call the wrong harmless to make the gift possible.

A gift can cost the giver dearly without becoming a debt owed to the one who receives it. So the criminal could receive what he could never demand.

For the same reason, a better moral record cannot establish a stronger right to Paradise. A person may have lived more honourably than the criminal, and that difference may have mattered a great deal to the people around them. It does not make Christ’s welcome a debt God owes.

Our acceptance rests on Jesus Christ and His saving work, received by grace. But how does a person come to receive what Christ has accomplished?

Faith That Receives

Paul says salvation is “by grace… through faith.” Ephesians 2:8. The criminal’s appeal lets us hear what that means in a particular life. He acknowledges his guilt, recognises Jesus’ innocence and asks Him to remember him.

He does not give himself a place in Paradise by speaking. He turns to the One he believes can receive him, and Jesus answers. Faith matters because of the Person in whom it is placed.

John Wesley, commenting on Ephesians 2:8, presents faith as the means by which we receive God’s gift, without any claim of personal merit. It is like an empty hand extended to receive something precious. The hand receives the gift, but doesn’t contribute anything towards its purchase.

We must not turn even that empty hand into an accomplishment. One person trusts Christ amid fear and uncertainty; another speaks with great confidence. The strength of either person’s feeling adds nothing to Christ’s power to save. The weight rests on Him.

Set the two appeals side by side. The criminal asks, “Lord, remember me.” Luke 23:42. The claimants ask, “Have we not…?” Matthew 7:22. The first turns towards Christ. The second turns towards works offered for His recognition.

That is no formula for judging anyone by a few spoken words. A faithful person may recount work done in Christ’s name; another may ask for mercy without trusting the One he addresses. The verdict is Christ’s to give.

Faith means placing our trust in Christ. Reliance of that kind has consequences when the One we trust speaks to us. What, then, do we make of His words about doing His Father’s will?

Known by Christ

The force of Christ’s reply to the claimants lies in what He refuses to recognise. Their appeal rests on a record of religious activity and would be persuasive to us. Christ’s reply begins, “I never knew you.” Matthew 7:23

He does not tell them the list is too short. He denies the relationship they presumed to have with Him. No further item could overturn that answer.

A person can do work under another’s name without being known by that person. The work may benefit others and earn their thanks. It does not establish the relationship claimed.

Christ is no distant employer waiting to learn whether the work happened. He knows what the claimants have done and how they have lived. We know only what Matthew gives us: their plea, His statement that He never knew them, and His description of them as workers of iniquity. We should not invent a private history for any of them.

What we can see is the difference between invoking Christ’s name and placing our trust in Him. The claimants appeal on the strength of works performed in His name, while the criminal asks for a welcome he cannot secure for himself. We do not know all that passed within their hearts. We do know that Christ answered them differently.

To be known by Christ speaks of a personal relationship. Jesus Himself connects that relationship with hearing His voice and following Him:

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” John 10:27

The sheep do not earn His acceptance by following Him. They follow because they hear His voice. The Christ in whom they place their trust is also the One who speaks of doing His Father’s will.

With this in mind, consider His warning in Matthew 7:

“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” Matthew 7:21

Obedience cannot be set aside to make grace more generous, and it cannot become an additional payment for God's gift. It belongs to the life that His grace makes possible.

The Life That Follows

Ephesians does not end with “not of works.” Paul immediately describes those saved by grace as God’s workmanship, “created in Christ Jesus unto good works” (Ephesians 2:10).

Good works are part of the life God intends for those who belong to Christ. They are not incidental to faith. They are also not something believers may disregard. But Paul’s order must be preserved. What follows salvation cannot be made the basis on which God grants it.

James confronts those who profess faith but leave a person in need without assistance:

“What doth it profit, my brethren, though a man say he hath faith, and have not works? can faith save him?” James 2:14

A brother or sister is without adequate clothing or daily food. Someone offers words of comfort but provides nothing to relieve their need. What value does such a profession of faith have when the person in front of us stays hungry?

James later declares, “I will shew thee my faith by my works” (James 2:18). We cannot dismiss his challenge by insisting that works do not earn salvation, only to walk past someone who needs food.

James questions whether a profession of faith is supported by the life of the person making it. Paul teaches that those saved by grace are created for good works. Neither allows us to overlook the person in need while debating the place of works in salvation.

Consider any genuine relationship. The way a person listens, responds and acts over time may reveal its depth and sincerity. Such conduct is not the price paid to secure it.

This makes none of us a judge over another person’s life. We overlook quiet obedience and mistake visible activity for devotion. Christ knows what remains hidden from us, and Matthew 7 has already shown that an impressive record does not settle the question.

The criminal had scarcely any time left to demonstrate what a life of following Jesus might have become. His lack of opportunity cannot serve as an excuse for those who have been given years to live in obedience.

The Deeds That Will Be Judged

One difficulty remains. If God welcomes by grace through faith, why does Scripture speak of judgment according to works?

Paul writes that God “will render to every man according to his deeds” (Romans 2:6). He also reminds believers that they must appear before Christ’s judgment seat, where their conduct in this life will be examined, “whether it be good or bad” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

The apostle who excludes boasting in works does not suggest that the life a person has lived will escape judgment. People have been helped or harmed, and duties kept or neglected. God can judge those deeds truthfully while receiving a sinner by grace in Christ.

Judgment according to deeds is not the same as earning acceptance before God. The former affirms that our conduct remains accountable to Him. The latter assumes that our works establish a right to His welcome, a claim Ephesians rejects.

Christians have differed over how faith, grace, obedience and final judgment relate, and it would be unfair to assert that every tradition which speaks strongly of obedience teaches that Paradise can be bought with deeds.

These passages do not permit an easy conclusion. Grace does not set aside Christ’s command to do the Father’s will, James’s warning against faith without works or Paul’s teaching on judgment. Neither can those teachings justify placing our confidence in our accomplishments rather than in Christ.

The people in Matthew 7 appeal to works performed in Christ’s name. He declares that He never knew them and identifies them as workers of iniquity. Their account of religious service cannot overturn His judgment of their conduct and it cannot establish the relationship He denies. Scripture doesn't permit us to dismiss every work they mention as false or to assume that no one benefited from their efforts.

The claimants’ rejection and the criminal’s welcome lead us towards the same conclusion from different directions. How a person lives matters, but the visible record of that life cannot, by itself, secure Christ’s acceptance. He knows the person before Him far better than we do.

John Calvin observed that Ephesians moves straight from excluding works as a claim to salvation to describing people created in Christ for good works. Grace gives rise to the life God calls a person to live.

Christ is the ground of God’s welcome. Faith receives His gift, which cannot be earned. The person who trusts Him is called to hear His voice and live accordingly, and the deeds of that life are not hidden from His judgment.

The criminal could build no future record; he could only entrust himself to Jesus. Most people who turn to Christ wake the next morning with relationships and responsibilities still before them.

What should the grace that received the criminal produce in a life given time to live?

sections.title: The Time the Criminal Never Had
sections.html:
The criminal did not have long to live after Christ promised him Paradise. We hear his admission of guilt, his appeal to Jesus and the answer he received. We cannot watch him return home, meet the people who knew him or decide how to live the next morning. There was no next morning for him.

That is the question in this chapter’s title. What if he had lived? Christ said, “To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” Luke 23:43. We cannot give the criminal another ending. We can ask what Scripture says to people who turn to Christ and are given years in which to live.

His final hours show that later good works were not a condition of his welcome. Most of us must go on living after we first turn to Christ. Our chance to act does not become irrelevant because he had none.

Suppose Tomorrow Came

For us, tomorrow often does come. We return to our families, our work and the people affected by our choices. We may have debts to pay, promises to keep and wrongs we can still put right.

Had the criminal lived, Christ’s promise would not have awaited a sufficient record of obedience. It would have been no permission to return to the conduct that brought him to Calvary.

Paul asks the question that follows naturally from grace:

“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” Romans 6:1–2

He goes on to describe those united with Christ as called to “walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). That new life comes through Christ. To continue deliberately in the old ways, without concern or repentance, would be difficult to reconcile with belonging to Him.

The criminal’s account offers no reason to delay repentance. He turned to Christ when he had the opportunity; none of us is assured of such an opportunity at the end of life.

The absence of subsequent good works cannot be held against him. He had no years left in which to serve, give or make amends. Christ knew his circumstances when He promised him Paradise.

Our circumstances are different. We do not obey to persuade Christ to make a promise He has already made. We have a life in which our response to Him can take shape.

The Work of a Continuing Life

Writing to the believers in Philippi, Paul urges them to continue in obedience, even in his absence. He calls them to take seriously the salvation they have received and to allow its implications to shape their conduct:

“Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.” Philippians 2:12

He is calling them to live out what God has already begun in them, with reverence and a proper sense of responsibility. His next sentence explains why such obedience is possible:

“For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.” Philippians 2:13

The believer is called to act, but is not left to personal strength alone. God Himself is at work, shaping both the desire to obey and the ability to carry it out.

Ordinary life bears this out. If a person feeds a hungry neighbour, the neighbour has been helped. If she keeps a difficult promise, someone has been spared the harm of a broken one.

James’s warning about offering kind words while leaving someone without food reminds us that the opportunity to help calls for action (James 2:14–17). A profession of faith cannot satisfy an empty stomach.

We cannot prescribe a minimum number of good deeds by which anyone earns Christ’s welcome. But years of persistent indifference to His voice raise legitimate questions about the faith a person professes. The criminal had no years in which his response could be observed. Most of us have been given that time.

The matter becomes more urgent when we still have the means to remedy the harm we have caused.

When Wrong Can Be Repaired

We do not know what offence brought the criminal under Roman judgment. Suppose only that someone turning to Christ today has taken what belongs to another person and still possesses it. What should happen tomorrow?

Keeping the property while saying, “Christ has forgiven me,” is no defence. Grace would then be protecting the very wrong the person claims to have left behind.

Zacchaeus gives us a concrete example. After receiving Jesus, he says: “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.” Luke 19:8

Jesus then declares: “This day is salvation come to this house…” Luke 19:9

Luke places Zacchaeus’s response to his possessions and his treatment of others beside Christ’s declaration of salvation. Repayment was not a price paid to obtain Jesus, but his encounter with Him touched the money he held and the people he may have wronged.

Zacchaeus’s example matters because he was still in a position to make amends. He could account for what he had taken, restore what was owed and change his dealings with others. Restitution could not erase his wrongdoing, but it could address losses that were still within his power to remedy.

The principle is wider than property. A lie may need correcting. A debt may need paying. An apology may be owed. Changing a settled pattern of conduct is often harder than any single act of repair, and it matters just as much to those who live with its consequences.

As a lawyer, I would also ask whose interests the proposed restitution is intended to serve. An offender may wish to apologise immediately, partly to relieve his own conscience. The person wronged may need time, distance or protection. Repentance does not entitle the offender to determine when, or whether, trust should be restored.

Had the criminal survived and been able to make restitution, Christ’s promise would not have relieved him of that responsibility. He would still have owed an honest response to anyone he had wronged, without needing to earn the place in Paradise already promised to him.

When Repair Has Limits

Some harm cannot be undone. A person may confess a lie without recovering the opportunity it cost someone else. Money can sometimes be returned; years of fear or a damaged relationship cannot be handed back in the same way.

Repentance keeps its meaning, but what it can do changes. A person may tell the truth, accept a lawful consequence, stop a harmful practice and respect the boundaries of someone who no longer feels safe with him.

Forgiveness before God does not require another person to resume trust. Some relationships should not return to what they were. A person who says he has changed may need to accept that others cannot yet see enough reason to believe him.

Christians who celebrate the criminal’s welcome should remain mindful of these distinctions. We do not know whom he may have wronged. We cannot presume that those affected would have been willing to meet him, much less insist that they owed him reconciliation because Christ had promised him Paradise.

The years remaining to us may bring difficult and humbling obligations. Making amends requires more than an apology. It may involve listening to those who suffered, repairing what can still be repaired and accepting consequences without regarding them as a denial of God’s grace.

None of this earns Christ’s welcome retrospectively. These responsibilities belong to the life that follows repentance, lived among neighbours whose interests remain worthy of our concern.
