When We Fail Again

A continuing life also brings continuing failure. Someone who meant to change may speak carelessly again, neglect a duty or discover that an old habit has more hold on him than he supposed.

We should not describe Christian growth as though one sincere beginning makes the years that follow flawless. John writes:

“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” 1 John 1:8

His next words open the way back:

“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” 1 John 1:9

Confession does not diminish the seriousness of repeated wrongdoing. It acknowledges the offence without excuse and turns to God rather than seeking to justify conduct we have been called to abandon. Where others have suffered harm, confession before God does not relieve us of the responsibility to make amends where we still can.

Paul tells the Corinthians:

“Know ye not that the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom of God?” 1 Corinthians 6:9

After naming forms of wrongdoing, he says, “And such were some of you.” 1 Corinthians 6:11. Their past did not put them beyond Christ’s reach, but neither did Paul give them leave to treat their former way of life as something they may continue without concern.

Jesus links fruitfulness to abiding in Him (John 15:1–6). The branch draws its life from the vine, and its fruit reveals something of that dependence. We must heed the warning. Uneven growth in another person is no ground for us to pronounce judgment on them.

A person may confess the same wrongdoing repeatedly before a pattern begins to change. An apology may need to be followed by a better decision tomorrow, and another the day after. Progress may be slow, even discouraging to the person striving for it, without being any less genuine.

Gradual growth is no excuse for a person to keep harming others while demanding them to endure it patiently. Where protection or a lawful consequence is needed, neither should be withheld. The responsibility to change remains with the person who committed the wrong.

Scripture’s warnings call for seriousness. They give us no private scoring system for counting another person’s failures and deciding whether Christ knows him. They ask us to listen to the One we say we trust, to repent when we fail and to take the people affected by our conduct seriously.

The Years We Have

The criminal’s final hours raise a question for those granted years after turning to Christ. If salvation is received by grace, what place does obedience have in the life that follows? Paul addresses this in his letter to Titus, where he describes grace as a teacher:

“For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.” Titus 2:11–12

The grace that welcomes us also teaches us how to live. Paul places that learning “in this present world,” amid our daily responsibilities, relationships and choices.

The years granted to us offer opportunities the criminal never had. They may hold service, generosity and faithful duties, but also failures requiring confession, wrongs to repair and renewed efforts to live differently.

Those years do not improve upon Christ’s promise. They matter because they are lived in response to Him. Their length gives us no greater claim upon His welcome, and no licence to treat what we do with them as inconsequential.

The criminal had no tomorrow in which we could watch his response unfold. We have ours. His story has shown us where our hope must rest; the life that follows asks whether we are listening to the One in whom we place it.

We cannot know what the criminal would have done with a tomorrow. We can ask what we have done with ours.

sections.title: A Mirror of Calvary
sections.html:
For much of this enquiry, someone else has stood before us. We listened to the criminal admit his guilt, heard the Pharisee pray and considered the works presented by the people in Matthew 7. Their words gave us questions to ask and let us remain observers for a time.

That distance has served its purpose. A mirror asks something different of us. We must recognise ourselves in the questions we have been asking about others. What do we expect to speak for us before Christ, and what happens to that confidence when we listen to His words?

Paul’s instruction is direct:

“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.” 2 Corinthians 13:5

The instruction includes the person writing these pages. An author gains no advantage before Christ by describing His grace, and a reader gains none merely by agreeing with the argument.

We Enter the Mirror

Luke records the criminal’s admission:

“And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds…” Luke 23:41

Many of us can identify real differences between his life and our own. We may never have been convicted of a crime. We may have worked honestly, cared for our families, kept difficult promises and tried to leave the people around us better than we found them.

Such distinctions matter. A person spared from harm has reason to value another’s restraint, just as a family faithfully provided for has reason to appreciate years of sacrifice. The criminal’s welcome does not erase the difference between conduct that benefits others and conduct that causes harm.

The difficulty arises when we treat that difference as grounds for claiming God’s acceptance. “We have lived better than that man” may be entirely true. But what does it establish about our standing before Christ?

The Pharisee’s prayer shows how easily another person can become useful to our confidence:

“God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are…” Luke 18:11

We need not repeat his words to adopt his method. We can think of someone whose wrongdoing is more public, whose failures are more damaging or whose beliefs appear less respectable, and feel quietly reassured. The comparison gives us relief without requiring us to consider what remains wrong in ourselves.

The criminal serves that purpose well. His guilt is admitted, his punishment visible and his circumstances safely removed from ordinary respectability. Standing beside him, most of us can produce something favourable to say about ourselves.

Paul leaves us no refuge in such comparisons:

“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” Romans 3:23

He does not suggest that everyone has committed the same offences or inflicted equal harm. Those differences cannot excuse our own sin. Another person’s greater wrongdoing cannot turn our dishonesty into truth, our cruelty into kindness or our hidden resentment into innocence.

This is where Calvary becomes a mirror. We begin to recognise the desire to have our lives assessed through the evidence most favourable to us. We remember the circumstances surrounding our failures and the effort behind our achievements, and hope that the resulting account will be sufficient.

There is nothing wrong with wanting a fair hearing. Human judgments should consider evidence, distinguish responsibility and resist careless accusations. But even the fairest account of our lives cannot turn what we have done wrong into something we have done right.

As a lawyer, I understand that every allegation must be examined for what the evidence establishes and what it leaves unproved. A person may rightly defeat a particular charge because the evidence does not support it. But before God, successfully answering an accusation would not settle the question of our own wrongdoing, which He knows in full.

We cannot limit the record to what speaks in our favour. There are words we have forgotten that others still remember, kindnesses received without gratitude and injuries we were quicker to justify than acknowledge to those affected. Even with sincere intentions, our understanding of ourselves remains incomplete.

That limitation should make us cautious about condemning others and about acquitting ourselves too readily. The criminal has occupied the dock long enough. His guilt cannot become our defence. On what, then, does our own confidence rest?

The Records We Bring

Most of us have a substantial record to consider. It contains duties fulfilled, opportunities wasted, sacrifices quietly made and decisions we would prefer not to revisit. Any examination worth the name must let the whole of that life come into view.

Much of it is good. Years spent caring for an ill relative have value. So do honest work, faithful parenting, generosity towards a neighbour and the refusal to exploit someone who could not have resisted.

Some of that goodness has been costly. A person may have remained dependable through exhaustion, provided for others at the expense of personal comfort or kept a promise long after keeping it ceased to bring pleasure. No one who benefited from it would say that such faithfulness meant nothing.

The trouble is what we begin to expect from it. Gratitude for an opportunity to serve can gradually become a claim upon the God before whom we serve. We may move from being thankful that something good was accomplished to believing that our contribution must secure His welcome.

Religious life brings its own risk. Church membership, baptism, prayer, giving and service are matters to take seriously. Through the Church we receive teaching, correction, fellowship and opportunities to care for people whose burdens we might otherwise never encounter.

Familiarity can make examination seem unnecessary. We know the language, recognise the passages and understand what a Christian answer should sound like. Others may trust our judgment, seek our prayers or regard us as examples of faith.

That confidence can be difficult to question because so much of it concerns things that are good. We should want to pray, serve and grow in understanding. The danger appears when our participation becomes the reason we think Christ could have no grounds to refuse us.

My own responsibilities make this question personal. Legal practice, writing, CMF’s work and the preservation of my father’s legacy all involve people with real needs. Marriage and fatherhood bring duties more intimate than any public undertaking.

These responsibilities demand my service, but they also provide achievements I might be tempted to claim. Have I not served my clients, written these books, helped these children and cared for my family? Even this brief account reveals how easily service can become a claim to merit.

Others will bring very different accounts. Some have little public achievement because caring for someone else consumed the years in which recognition might have come. Some have lived generously outside any religious community, while others have served within the Church for as long as they can remember.

No one needs to borrow another person’s record for this examination. The question finds us in the lives we have lived. What have we done that matters, and what have we begun to believe it entitles us to receive?

The claimants in Matthew 7 give that expectation its unsettling expression:

“Have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?” Matthew 7:22

We have already considered their appeal in its own setting. Here its force lies in the confidence with which they expect their works to settle the matter. What they present appears sufficient to them.

Their words are no weapon against everyone who serves publicly or speaks gratefully of what God has enabled. They are no distant warning about other people, either. They ask us to examine the conclusion we draw from our own service.

Do we receive opportunities to do good as responsibilities entrusted to us? Or do we quietly accumulate them as reasons why rejection should be impossible? The difference may remain hidden until we feel overlooked, corrected or treated less favourably than someone whose record we consider inferior.

Our response to another person’s mercy can be revealing. We may welcome grace in principle and still resent its generosity towards someone who has contributed less. Their welcome can seem to diminish the value of our own years of faithfulness.

Those we have helped have been helped. The promises we honoured still matter to those who relied on them. Another person’s experience of mercy does not undo that good; it challenges what we believed our good conduct entitled us to receive.

This examination is also for those burdened by their own past. Shame can keep our attention fixed on our earlier failures. Some may regard their wrongdoing as too grave for Christ to receive them.

Such consciences need patient care. Sin is serious, but its seriousness does not make forgiveness impossible. The criminal’s appeal sends us back to the One who heard and answered him.

Paul calls us to examine whether we are in the faith. That requires more than deciding whether we feel pleased or disappointed with the lives we have lived. We must ask whom we trust, how we receive His words and what we do when those words expose something we would rather defend.

Before the Same Christ

Self-examination must lead somewhere. If we remain absorbed in ourselves, we may spend a lifetime reviewing the evidence without becoming any more willing to listen to Christ. What we discover must shape our response to Him.

One question gets to the point. When we recognise wrongdoing in our lives, what do we do with it?

We may compare ourselves favourably with those who have done worse, or invoke our generosity as though it could excuse other wrongs. We may defend our intentions so thoroughly that the person we harmed is almost forgotten.

Or we may acknowledge what happened, seek forgiveness and address what can still be put right. An apology, restitution or a necessary change in conduct can make repentance costly. We begin to face the wrong when we accept responsibility for its consequences.

Even then, we cannot purchase mercy through the thoroughness of our repentance. Confession brings us before Christ with what we need forgiven. It gives us no reason to admire ourselves for having made it.

Some readers already scrutinise every motive and revisit every failure. A call to self-examination may seem to demand another round of that exhausting enquiry. They need to remember that a believer may stumble, grieve over the failure and return to Christ.

We need not understand ourselves perfectly before trusting Him. Obedience may be sincere even when our motives are mixed. We remain dependent on His mercy throughout the examination.

Others need a more searching question. Can a decision made years ago justify indifference to Christ today? Grace is no reason to disregard what He now requires of us.

Jesus says:

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” John 10:27

His words point to a living relationship in which His voice matters. Do we listen when obedience is inconvenient, receive correction when it is needed and return to Him when we have wandered?

Following Him takes place within the lives still entrusted to us. It may mean returning to work with greater honesty, attending to a neglected family member or ending a habit of evasion. The responsibilities waiting for us when this book closes are part of our answer to its questions.

Our dealings with others come into view as well. If another person’s guilt cannot serve as our defence, it should stop being a source of satisfaction. If our service puts God under no obligation, it is no weapon for diminishing someone else.

We can honour faithfulness without ranking ourselves for admission to Paradise. We can name wrongdoing, seek justice for those harmed and recognise that mercy reaches people whose histories trouble us. Holding these together is difficult, and the difficulty is a reason for humility.

Whatever time remains gives us responsibilities the criminal never had the opportunity to fulfil. There is work to continue, harm to stop and good to undertake. Faithful service stands, and failure does not end the possibility of change.

We have heard enough to make observing from a distance inadequate. The enquiry concerns the confidence with which we live, how we repent and the attention we give to Christ. It includes both the reader who has followed the argument and the author who has tried to make it clear.

The Lord of Both Verdicts

We began with a criminal who acknowledged his guilt and received from Christ a promise of Paradise. How could someone condemned for his wrongdoing be welcomed into God’s Kingdom? The question seemed to concern one man and the mercy shown to him.

In Matthew 7 we met people who expected a very different verdict. They spoke of prophecy, deliverance and wonderful works performed in Christ’s name, and the Lord they claimed to serve answered, “I never knew you.”

Set side by side, the two scenes brought us to examine the grounds of our own confidence before God. Scripture takes human conduct seriously without making it the price of salvation. The life we lead remains accountable to God, and our hope of being received rests upon Christ.

The scandals of grace and entitlement reveal no contradiction in God’s justice. The criminal acknowledged his guilt and entrusted himself to Christ, receiving a promise he could never have earned.

Those who invoked the Lord’s name appealed to their works, only to discover that these could not establish the relationship they presumed. Their accomplishments gave them no claim to salvation, just as the criminal’s guilt did not place him beyond mercy.

The two verdicts bring us to the same unsettling truth: what ultimately matters is whether we are known by Christ and have placed our trust in Him.

We cannot borrow the criminal’s final hour or claim his history as our own. We can approach the same Saviour with the failures we cannot undo, the good for which we are grateful and whatever years remain.

Before Him, having written this book gives me no advantage over those who read it. We stand before Him alike, each known more completely than any account we could offer of ourselves.

The criminal asked to be remembered. Christ answered with a promise greater than his request. The same Lord declares:

“…him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” John 6:37

So we come to Him in repentance and trust His word. Our remaining years give us opportunities to follow Him, fulfil our responsibilities and make amends where we can. We do these things because His grace has reached us, not to persuade Him that we deserve it.

The man on the cross had no defence to offer. Those who cried “Lord, Lord” believed they had much to present.

The criminal died under a sentence he acknowledged as deserved. He could not undo his past or change the judgment of those who condemned him. But he had turned to the innocent Man beside him, and that Man had promised him Paradise.

There is much still to learn about the mystery of the God who pronounced both verdicts.

sections.title: Epilogue
sections.subtitle: The Greatest Surprise in Heaven
sections.html:
This enquiry began with two troubling answers from the same Christ. He welcomed a condemned criminal and refused people who appealed to works done in His name. Their records did not lead to the verdicts my understanding of justice and deserving had prepared me to expect.

Growing up among people whose faith shaped their daily choices taught me how the expectation of Heaven could influence life on earth. Their enthusiasm was not always mine, but their conviction stayed with me through the years. Being with Christ was something worth living for.

Time has given those memories a different weight. The question of whom Christ receives into Heaven, and on what basis, has not gone away.

My legal training made it difficult to accept any explanation that overlooked either the harm wrongdoing causes or the value of faithful service. Both had to be accounted for.

At Calvary, the difficulty was how mercy could reach the criminal without leaving justice unanswered. Looking more closely at the Saviour beside him showed what his record alone could never explain. Christ Himself bore the cost of the welcome.

Christ’s refusal of the claimants challenged a different expectation. The good they presented could have value without entitling them to Paradise. Together, these answers brought me to the heart of the apparent contradictions that had first troubled me.

I had to question my own method as well. The desire to understand Christ’s answers had sat alongside an expectation that they would confirm my own conclusions.

Even understanding these verdicts can leave another confidence untouched. We picture unexpected people being welcomed into Heaven and seemingly certain entrants absent. In that imagined scene, we have already placed ourselves safely inside, marvelling at how mistaken everyone else has been.

My own place in that picture could no longer remain unquestioned.

What about you, nwoke m?

Recognising misplaced confidence in others had not made my own easier to question. Christ already knew the life behind any account of mine, including the failures more readily explained than acknowledged.

Odera’s passing made the distinction between a life remembered and a life before God more real to me. Gratitude for my father’s life continues through work intended to benefit others. That work honours his legacy; it cannot establish his standing before God.

The same is true of my own work. One day, others may preserve something of it. A book may still encourage a reader, a project may continue to meet a need, and something taught to my son may guide him when my voice is no longer there to offer counsel.

Those possibilities give me reasons to work faithfully now. But the good that survives me cannot secure my welcome before Christ. I must depend upon the Saviour whom these efforts may help others come to know.

I can no longer think of Heaven’s greatest surprise merely in terms of the people we might find there. My attention turns towards the God we aspire to be with, whose ways have already challenged my reckoning.

Receiving what He reveals requires openness to answers that may unsettle familiar convictions. The questions are welcome. So is the possibility that His words will change the person asking them.

That learning must continue beyond this manuscript. My family, legal practice, business and foundation responsibilities are still mine to carry. Knowing that my works cannot purchase salvation makes none of them unimportant; it changes what I ask them to secure.

Our hope remains in Jesus Christ. His grace gives no ground for disregarding His judgment; His judgment gives no ground for diminishing His grace.

The way forward, for author and reader alike, is to bring our questions to Christ without disguise and let what we learn of Him shape our choices and responsibilities.

I began this enquiry wanting to understand why Christ welcomed a criminal and refused people whose welcome seemed more likely. I close more conscious of my own need for Him, and of how much knowing Him must shape the life still before me.

My prayer for us remains that we may entrust ourselves to Jesus Christ and His saving grace, grow in our knowledge of our Father and His ways, and live purposefully under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Amen and Amen.

sections.title: Benediction
sections.html:
May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,

The Love of God,

And the sweet fellowship of the Holy Spirit,

Abide with us all, today and forever,

Amen.

Adapted from 2 Corinthians 13:14

sections.title: Appendix I
sections.subtitle: Key Scriptures on Grace, Faith and Works
sections.html:
This guide gathers the passages most useful for revisiting the book’s central question: upon what basis does anyone enter the Kingdom of God? Read each passage in its setting. The distinction running through this enquiry is between what Christ gives, how a person receives it and how that person lives when given time to follow Him.

The Promise at Calvary

Luke 23:39–43 — The criminal acknowledges his guilt, speaks of Jesus’ innocence and asks to be remembered. Christ promises that he will be with Him in Paradise that day.

1 Peter 3:18 — Peter describes the just Christ suffering for the unjust “that he might bring us to God.”

Grace and the Ground of Acceptance

Romans 3:23–26 — Paul brings human sin, free justification, Christ’s redemption and God’s justice into the same account. This is a principal passage for the question explored in Chapters Three and Five: how can God receive the guilty and remain just?

2 Corinthians 5:21 — Christ, who “knew no sin,” is central to the righteousness received “in him.”

Ephesians 2:8–10 — Salvation is God’s gift, received through faith and “not of works.” The passage continues by saying that believers are created in Christ Jesus “unto good works.”

Romans 4:4–5 — Paul distinguishes a wage owed for work from justification received through faith. The distinction helps explain why good works cannot put God in our debt.

Philippians 3:8–9 — Paul seeks to be found in Christ rather than to rest his standing before God on his own righteousness.

Faith and the One Trusted

Luke 23:42–43 — The criminal’s brief request directs our attention to the Person he addresses. Christ’s answer gives him more than he asked for.

Acts 16:30–31 — Asked what must be done to be saved, Paul and Silas direct the questioner to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.

John 5:21–22 — Jesus speaks of the Son’s authority to give life and the judgment committed to Him. His promise at Calvary rests upon His authority.

John 10:27–28 — Christ says that He knows His sheep, gives them eternal life and that they follow Him. The passage speaks both to assurance and to the life of those who hear His voice.

Good Works and the Life That Follows

Matthew 5:16 — Jesus calls His followers to good works through which others may glorify the Father.

Matthew 6:1–2 — Jesus warns against giving in order to receive human praise. A work may be seen; the question includes what the giver seeks from being seen.

Philippians 2:12–13 — Believers are told to work out their salvation, with the assurance that God is at work in them.

Titus 2:11–12 — The grace that brings salvation also teaches people how to live.

James 2:14–18, 24 — James challenges a claim to faith that has no living expression. His words require careful hearing alongside Paul’s refusal to make works the price of grace.

Luke 19:1–10 — Zacchaeus’s response to Jesus includes a commitment to give and to make restitution. His account helps us consider what repentance can look like when a person has a tomorrow.

Works, Judgment and Misplaced Confidence

Luke 18:9–14 — The Pharisee trusts in his own righteousness and compares himself with the publican. Jesus says that the man who asks for mercy goes home justified.

Matthew 7:21–23 — Jesus speaks both of doing the Father’s will and of people who appeal to works done in His name, yet hear, “I never knew you.” Neither part of His warning should be passed over.

Matthew 25:31–46 — Deeds of mercy appear in Jesus’ account of judgment. Their presence calls us to take conduct seriously without turning it into a purchase price for the Kingdom.

2 Corinthians 5:10 — Paul says that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ. The life lived matters, even though it cannot place Christ in anyone’s debt.

Reading the Passages Together

These Scriptures prevent us from making either of two easy claims. We cannot say that good works secure Christ’s welcome: the criminal’s promise and the warning in Matthew 7 will not allow it. Nor can we say that conduct ceases to matter once grace has been received: Jesus, Paul and James will not allow that either.

The order matters throughout: God gives salvation through Jesus Christ; faith receives what He gives; and, where life continues, grace calls forth a life of obedience. When the question is what can bear the weight of our acceptance before God, these passages direct us to Christ.

sections.title: Appendix II
sections.subtitle: Grace, Faith and Works: The Distinctions That Matter
sections.html:
Several terms used throughout this book are closely related but should not be confused.

Grace describes God's unmerited favour towards the sinner. Salvation originates in God and cannot be converted into a debt owed because the recipient has accumulated sufficient merit.

Faith is the means by which the gift is received. Christian faith is not confidence in the psychological strength of one's own believing; its saving significance lies in its object, Jesus Christ.

Repentance involves a genuine turning from sin towards God. The criminal's words reveal no attempt to excuse his guilt; where life continues, repentance should ordinarily become visible in a changed direction of life.

Justification concerns the sinner's acceptance as righteous before God through Christ. It is not the gradual accumulation of sufficient moral improvement.

Sanctification concerns the continuing work of God in the believer's life, producing growth in holiness and obedience. It follows grace rather than becoming the consideration by which grace is purchased.

Good works are commanded and valuable. They serve neighbours, glorify God and give visible expression to living faith. Scripture also speaks of human beings being judged according to their works. Their proper place is therefore substantial but carefully defined: they may be fruit, evidence and objects of judgment without becoming currency by which salvation is purchased.

Assurance rests ultimately upon Christ rather than upon the believer's ability to produce an impeccable spiritual résumé. Biblical assurance is not complacency: the Christ who knows His sheep also says that they hear His voice and follow Him. Evidence of grace may strengthen assurance, but evidence must never be made a substitute for Christ.

Perseverance describes continuing in faith and allegiance to Christ. Scripture repeatedly warns believers against drawing back, unbelief and settled disobedience, while also grounding their confidence in God's sustaining grace. Perseverance is therefore spiritually serious without becoming another purchase price for salvation.

Judgment according to works is a recurring biblical theme. It means that human conduct is not irrelevant to God's final judgment. It should not be confused with the different proposition that good works accumulate sufficient merit to place God under obligation to save.

These distinctions protect the Christian account from two opposite errors.

The first is legalism: the attempt to make human achievement part of the ground upon which God becomes obligated to save.

The second is licence: the claim that because salvation is by grace, obedience and the subsequent direction of a believer's life are spiritually irrelevant.

The New Testament permits neither.

“For by grace are ye saved through faith… Not of works, lest any man should boast.” Ephesians 2:8–9

Yet the sentence continues:

“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works…” Ephesians 2:10

The order is the distinction.

sections.title: Appendix III
sections.subtitle: Questions for Personal Reflection and Group Discussion
sections.html:
Using This Study Guide

These questions follow the enquiry from the criminal at Calvary to Christ’s warning in Matthew 7, and finally to the question of our own confidence before God. Return to the relevant chapters and Scriptures as you consider them. The personal questions invite an honest answer from within; the group questions are intended to help readers examine the passages together without requiring anyone to disclose more than they wish.

Personal Reflection

1.     When I hear that a condemned criminal was promised Paradise that day, what first troubles me about Christ’s welcome?

2.     Am I tempted to soften the criminal’s guilt, or to imagine offences Luke has not recorded? Why?

3.     What do I find hardest to say honestly about my own wrongdoing without immediately explaining or comparing it?

4.     When mercy reaches someone I would have placed last, do I welcome it or begin calculating what that person deserves?

5.     What difference does it make to my hope that Christ promised the criminal not merely Paradise, but “with me”?

6.     Where do I usually look for assurance when I have failed: to Christ’s promise, or to the apparent strength of my repentance and faith?

7.     Are there religious activities I have begun to treat as proof that Christ knows me, without listening seriously to what He says?

8.     Whose conduct do I compare with mine when I want to feel better about where I stand before God?

9.     What good work, act of service or sacrifice am I most tempted to enter in a private account of what God should think of me?

10.  Do I still value the good I do when nobody sees it, thanks me or remembers that I did it?

11.  Where life has given me time to obey or repair a wrong, have I used grace as a reason to act—or as a reason to delay?

12.  If I could offer no comparison, achievement or religious résumé before Christ, what would remain as the ground of my confidence?

Group Discussion

1.     Why do Christ’s promise to the criminal in Luke 23:43 and His verdict in Matthew 7:23 unsettle our ordinary expectations in opposite ways?

2.     Why does the criminal’s admission, “we indeed justly,” matter? What questions about his offence does Luke leave unanswered?

3.     How can concern for anyone harmed by a wrongdoer be taken seriously when discussing forgiveness before God?

4.     What do the criminal’s words show about his response to Jesus? Why can that response matter without becoming the price of Paradise?

5.     How do Isaiah 53, 1 Peter 3:18 and Romans 3:23–26 help explain how Christ can welcome the guilty while remaining just?

6.     What do Jonah’s anger and Isaiah’s invitation to the wicked reveal about the limits of human judgment?

7.     Why does the authority of the One who says “To day shalt thou be with me” matter more to the criminal’s assurance than anything he can now accomplish?

8.     In Matthew 7:21–23, why must we hear both “I never knew you” and Jesus’ words about doing the Father’s will?

9.     What is wrong with the Pharisee’s prayer in Luke 18 if some of the good conduct he describes may be real?

10.  How can a good work benefit another person and still become part of an unreliable plea before God? How do Matthew 5:16, 6:1–2 and 7:22 help answer that question?

11.  How can Ephesians 2:8–10 and James 2 help us distinguish the ground of salvation from the life that follows it?

12.  After hearing both verdicts, how would you answer the book’s governing question: upon what basis does anyone enter the Kingdom of God?

sections.html:
The Bible is the principal source for this enquiry. The Christian writers below are included where their comments help us consider the criminal’s appeal, Christ’s warning in Matthew 7, and the relationship between grace, faith and good works. Abraham Maslow appears separately: his account of human needs provides a way of considering our desire for recognition, rather than a theological explanation of why people do good.

Holy Scripture

The Holy Bible: King James Version. Originally published 1611.

Christian Sources and Related Reading

Augustine of Hippo. Our Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, especially his discussion of Matthew 5:16 and 6:1. Augustine considers why Jesus calls His followers to let their good works be seen while warning them against seeking praise through those works.

Augustine of Hippo. On Grace and Free Will, chapter 19. Augustine asks how eternal life can be spoken of as a reward for service while remaining a gift of grace. newadvent.org

Calvin, John. Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists: Matthew, Mark, and Luke, on Luke 18:14 and Luke 23:42–43.

Calvin, John. Commentaries on the Epistles of Paul, on Ephesians 2:8–10 and 2 Corinthians 13:5.

Chrysostom, John. On the Cross and the Thief. Chrysostom reflects on the condemned man’s words and the promise Christ made to him. catholiclibrary.org

Chrysostom, John. Homilies on the Gospel of Matthew, Homily 19, on Matthew 6:1–2. His discussion attends to the purpose for which an act of giving is made visible.

Henry, Matthew. An Exposition of the Old and New Testament, on Matthew 7:21–23 and Jonah 4. His comments help illuminate both Christ’s answer to the claimants and Jonah’s distress when Nineveh was spared. Bible Gateway

Spurgeon, Charles H. “The Believing Thief.” Sermon on Luke 23:42–43. Spurgeon reflects on the criminal as Christ’s companion at the gate of Paradise. The Spurgeon Library

Spurgeon, Charles H. “The Disowned.” Sermon on Matthew 7:21–23, delivered 22 April 1877. The Spurgeon Library

Wesley, John. Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament, on Ephesians 2:8 and 2 Corinthians 13:5.

Human Motivation Discussed in This Book

Maslow, Abraham H. “A Theory of Human Motivation.” Psychological Review 50, no. 4 (1943): 370–396. Maslow’s discussion of esteem and self-actualisation helps frame questions about achievement, recognition and the wish to be seen as one’s resources and responsibilities change. His proposed hierarchy should not be taken to mean that everyone develops the same motives in a fixed order, or that a good deed can be explained simply by its giver’s age. psychclassics.yorku.ca
